He'll jump away and send a wave of generic goons at you and toss in some easy to avoid bombs. You clear out the goons, Joker gets distracted by the evening news, and you take him down with the back claw and... pow. Repeat this two more times and you win. That's it. That's Batman's final challenge. Three waves of standard enemies and running around Joker a few times. As a culmination of the narrative and as a test of your accumulated skills, the Titan Joker fight falls flat on its face. Thankfully, Rocksteady did a much better job in Arkham City. Its final boss pits you against Clayface, this time set up by the Joker. It's a much better story hook, as having the Joker use other villains as part of his plan is much more in character for him. Clayface being revealed as Joker's body double is a cool surprise and recontextualizes the story so far. He feels like a natural part of the story. The two phase fight is pretty fun and works as a final test. In the first phase, Clayface keeps changing shape while attacking you with a variety of moves. He charges at you by rolling into a ball, he'll try to smash you from afar with his stretchy arms, he'll morph those arms into blades and slice you, he leaps at you with hammer arms, he throws wads of clay that you have to duck or leap over. You have to keep moving and stay on your toes while pelting him with ice bombs. Once you whittle his health down, he'll freeze up and you get to slice him to pieces with the sword lodged into his back. After a short scene, the second phase begins. Clayface is weakened and looks like he's falling apart. He sends waves of clay monsters that you slice up in the traditional free flow combat style. If you break it down, this phase is actually not that different from Titan Joker. Both fights have you fighting waves of normal enemies while the villain sends out projectiles. But it works so much better for the Clayface fight because of the better story context and the more interesting and challenging previous phase of the fight. It fits with the game's combat and works much better as an endurance battle. It's not the most amazing or difficult finale in the game, but the Clayface fight succeeds where Titan Joker failed. It's a good final challenge that has a healthy amount of variety. It uses its characters well and it fits naturally in the story. So Rocksteady learned from their mistakes, but now let's talk about two of the greatest bosses of all time, in the same game in fact. Metal Gear Solid 3 has two standout fights against The End and The Boss. The battles are designed as a midterm and a final exam for Metal Gear Solid's core stealth gameplay. Both are great fights, and for different reasons. The End for its mechanics, and The Boss for its build up and narrative. In the fight against The End, you face off against a legendary 100 year old sniper, clinging to life just long enough to face you. You use every stealth trick in your arsenal to search for him across three forested areas and take him down. Think find the needle in the haystack, but the needle is packing heat. This encounter is slow and intense in a way that not many other boss fights are. MGS3 is in love with clockwork gameplay systems, and the fight against The End encourages you to find where he's hiding in creative ways. You can spot the glare from his rifle, use the directional microphone to catch the faint sound of his breathing, use the thermal goggles to keep track of him as he moves to a new sniper's nest, or you could just capture and release his pet parrot, which flies right to him. Just like the other fights in the game, you can take him down with the usual lethal and non-lethal options. You can even get unique camo for sneaking up close to him and holding him up. This fight is full of cool little details and easter eggs. The game even gives you two ways to bypass the fight entirely. There's a brief window earlier in the game where you can take him out as he lingers in the environment immediately after a cutscene. Or do that fourth wall breaking trick that Kojima is known for. Start the fight, save, and set the system clock forward a week. The End will die of old age the next time you start the game. Countless other games have boss fights that force you down a single path to pass them. Action games sometimes give players some flexibility in which tools they use to get through a boss fight, but the fight against The End feels more immersive, taking place in a more realistic world where lateral thinking is rewarded and you're in control of the outcome. More so than the other more straightforward boss fights in MGS3, like the fear or the bees. A slow, intense sniper battle is a great change of pace that rewards creativity in ways that you rarely see, outside of other series built entirely around the concept, like Hitman or Dishonored. Metal Gear Solid has other boss fights with creative latitude, but the fight with The End gives that extra, unexpected degree of freedom. The sheer variety of paths you can go down makes for an unforgettable, unique encounter. The rare kind that you can tell as a story and hear the stories of other people, and share in the ways you overcame the challenge. Then we have the final battle with The Boss. Mechanically, it doesn't do nearly as much as the fight with The End. The fight itself isn't that different from the game's other fights either, but narratively, it's unmatched. The

## Final Fantasy IX - How to Pace a Game ~ Design Doc
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SKEp3fX1JT4

Hey, we're relaunching our Patreon. We have a new Patreon-exclusive behind-the-scenes Design Doc podcast, and we're putting early video access, credit shoutouts, and voting in lower backer tiers. If you like our videos, click the Patreon link in the description below to help support us and keep Design Doc rolling.
Square caught fire in the late 90s. Over five years, they released a string of four JRPG masterpieces back to back to back to back. Dozens of other studios have made countless JRPGs since then. Some have been great, some are a different kind of great. But Square's streak of speed and quality was unmatched from Final Fantasy VII through X. Yes, that includes the one with the gun hot-glued to a sword. Right in the middle of that streak was Final Fantasy IX. It wasn't the best-selling, but it sold well enough. It wasn't the best-looking of the four, but for a game on the original PlayStation, it looked great. It didn't have the best soundtrack. Wait, I take that back. Maybe it did. But it had a killer narrative and a very good level-up system. Let's dive into Final Fantasy IX and explore how Square created a gripping narrative, a tight gameplay loop, and talk about what it took to design Sakaguchi's masterpiece.
FF IX came out in the year 2000 and altogether sold about 6 million copies over its lifetime. Maybe a little more now with the new re-releases. It's beloved, critically acclaimed at release, and a fan favorite now. But it's the weakest selling of any of the 3D mainline single-player Final Fantasy games, from VII through XV. They're not bad sales numbers, but FF VII sold 13 million copies and VIII sold 9 million copies. FF IX just wasn't in the same ballpark.
The most astonishing thing about FF IX might be how quickly it came together. It came out barely a year after FF VIII, with only a few months of pre-production work on IX happening during the development of VIII. That's an astounding turnaround time for such a rich, fully-featured game. It's been a long time since top-end AAA game development could crank out a game in a little over a year, and Square hasn't come close to matching that since. In the time between FF XIII and XV, you could cram like four FF IX development cycles in there. Get those sequels out.
With its release date announced in the same press conference that introduced both Final Fantasy X and XI, FF IX was never given a chance to breathe. Too bad, because it was designed as a vision of where the series had come from and what it could be at its best. A beautiful fusion of classic sword and sorcery Final Fantasy and the system-heavy, story-driven epics of the more recent games.
By the time it was released, the PS2 was already out. FF X was less than a year away, and that had fancy new higher-resolution graphics and full voice acting. Not to mention a good story and fun gameplay in its own right. FF X was always destined to steal the spotlight. Even though it was buried by a hardware cycle, FF IX is still as good today as it was in 2000, just waiting to be discovered by new fans willing to seek it out. But what makes it a gem? FF IX has some of the best pacing in games, in its narrative and in its gameplay, especially for a game from around the year 2000, and certainly for a JRPG.
So what is narrative pacing anyway? It's plot crossed with timing. A story's plot will include things like a character's background, new locations to visit, new motivations, a fateful conversation between two characters, action scenes, romance, betrayal and redemption. But pacing isn't just about the plot. You can tell those same events in an infinite number of ways. Pacing is about how you pick and choose the events to show in your story. It can be sped up or slowed down depending on which events you show, which you leave out, and how they're told. In Skyrim, if you started the game with a prisoner cart ride that took two hours instead of a few minutes, the game's plot would be the same, but the pacing would be a disaster. Bad pacing bores the audience, and they might put your game down, never to pick it up again.
Final Fantasy IX is paced very well with an action-packed first few hours. The game opens with the lead-up to an elaborate stage play turned kidnapping scheme. You flip between Zidane, the thief and theater troupe member, Vivi, a lonely young black mage looking for a place to watch the show, and Steiner, the bumbling captain of Alexandria's Knights of Pluto. Each segment quickly introduces a chunk of the game's cast. You get just enough information to keep their immediate motivations in context without bogging down the story with irrelevant details. Vivi's story starts with him finding out his ticket to the play is fake, but you get the sense that Vivi is out of place, on a deeper level than just a counterfeit ticket, and then he gets accidentally swept up in the heist. You get clear goals for Zidane, Garnet, and Steiner, and an antagonist to root against in Queen Braune. Supporting characters like the tantalus group of thieves, the jesters, and Beatrix appear briefly to be fully integrated later.
You're introduced to the beautiful streets of Alexandria, filled with dozens of NPCs to give it vibrancy. Even the save system has a bit of depth to it, with the start of a subplot about the Moogle's mail delivery system. Within the first hour of play, you're led outside of the city and into a forest mini-dungeon and an ice cavern mini-dungeon. The characters start to flesh out their motivations and what they're immediately trying to do, and you start to have way more questions about Vivi. Oh boy, that's uh, that's rough bud.
Through the first two hours, you've already met most of the game's major players. You were exposed to tons of story hooks, you've played through two dungeons, and have gotten used to the battle system. These story beats are made up of just a few sentences, but they paint the world in surprising detail. Each new segment opens the door to a little more of a character's true depth and personality. You zip between groups and plot hooks so quickly that the game never feels like it has stalled out, or started to flood you with one big exposition dump. It lets the intrigue of the Mist Continent and the world of Gaia develop gradually, but steadily in the background.
Most of the rest of the modern Final Fantasy games take a longer time to get into gear. FF13's 20-hour tutorial is the most famous and worst example. FF8 gives you a battle system and story exposition dump back-to-back at the very start. FF10 was a slower burn, meandering for two or three hours after an explosive beginning. FF15 is actually close to FF9 in its early game pacing, with a more reasonable 20-ish minutes to get into the action. Throughout the first two discs of FF9, the stakes steadily build, alliances develop and deepen, the antagonists reveal themselves and evolve. The game's expert pacing keeps players in the flow of the story, and before you know it, you're fully committed to the complex world of Final Fantasy IX.
So, FF9's narrative pacing is phenomenal, and if it were a novel or a TV series, that would be the start and end of it. But games are different. Games are interactive, and there's a different sort of pacing that games can use, beyond their story. Many designers call it the gameplay loop. It's the moment-to-moment game actions you're taking as a player. Just like how well-designed narrative pacing in a story can make it easier to stay invested in the world, the gameplay loop can make it easier to stay invested in the action.
Jamie Griesemer, formerly a Bungie, coined the phrase 30 seconds of fun to describe the gameplay loop they designed while creating Halo. Halo's 30 seconds of fun was a series of actions that you would take over and over again while you were playing the game. The context, the stuff happening around that loop, would change a little bit each time, but that core would stay roughly the same. Halo's loop was centered around how to take out a group of enemies. You'd sneak up on one and melee them, toss a grenade towards another group, and clean up whoever was left. Surrounding that loop, there would be little tweaks as you progressed through the game. The makeup of the enemies would change a bit, the level layouts would be different, the backdrop might be different, but you'd still be using grenades, guns, and melee attacks as core actions. Crowd control, cover, and weak points.
Getting that loop to be fun was perhaps the most important thing in the game's design. It did the heavy lifting to hold the player's attention. If the loop was dull, the fundamental core of the game would be dull too, and people would quit. With an engaging loop and enough interesting little twists on the periphery, they could keep the momentum of the game going. That's how a game can hold a player's attention through hour one, hour five, and hour 100.
So, what's FF9's gameplay loop then? You've got the usual turn-based JRPG battle mechanics on one hand. Wait your turn and punch some monsters. Get experience when you win, then level up. Basic stuff. But it turns out that surface level grind isn't all that important in FF9. It's not that difficult to keep your character levels very low and still win the game. There's another more important mechanic that helps pace the game just like the narrative loop does. FF9 has an AP system that combines skills and equipment into a system that keeps your interest and feeds right back into the basic JRPG combat loop.
Every weapon, piece of armor, or accessory you can equip has a set of abilities. There's spells,

## Good Design, Bad Design Vol. 5 - The Best and Worst of Video Game Graphic Design ~ Design Doc
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ubkf0_qYQMc

Hey, guess what? It's time for another Good Design, Bad Design, where we talk about graphic design in games. A game's graphic design is a close cousin to a game's art overall, but graphic design is focused on visual communication. Things like menus, UI, camera work, color choice, font choice, animation, character design, the presentation of information. Also, keep in mind, good graphic design can happen in bad games, and good games can have bad graphic design. So with that said, let's get going. Good Design After the graphic design mess that was Smash 4, the menus and interface of Super Smash Bros. Ultimate wins the award for most improved. Smash Ultimate's style and presentation is more striking this time. Series director Masahiro Sakurai is on record saying that he took notice of Persona 5's dynamic interface, and it shows. Sakurai's Persona 5 inspirations shine through in the new victory screen animations. The composition and the way everything snaps into place take major cues from Persona 5's all-out attacks, and they look fantastic. The main menu layouts and transitions are sleeker, again taking inspiration from Persona. The transitions are quick and dynamic, stylishly moving from menu to menu. The camera zooms in and uses the negative space of the option icons to frame each submenu. It's a clever balance of style and functionality. I mentioned in the very first Bad Design segment that Smash 4's organization and visual hierarchy were a mess, so it's great to see Ultimate make some major improvements. The submenu options are placed where they should be. Things are much easier to find. The most prominent options are Smash and Spirits, which hold the main local and single-player adventure modes respectively, but the options also don't overpower the menu. They even changed the Games & More section to an organized collection of the old classic game modes, away from the earlier game's random hodgepodge of options. I still hate that title, but hey, it's accurate now. The in-game HUD got great quality of life improvements. There are new UI elements like a stage map to show how close you are to blast zones. They also added new elements for character-specific mechanics, like the Inkling's ink meter, the Villager's pocketed items, and Robin's weapon durability. The end of a match even spices things up with a dynamic zoom-in on finishing blows. Smash Ultimate's interface is so much better, but the usability still has some room to improve. So, it's time for a tiny bad design. Tiny bad design. There are a few little things that make navigation feel just a bit more cumbersome than necessary. Saving your custom rulesets is a great new feature, but you can't make minor edits like item settings, stock numbers, or the stage hazard toggle in the rules from the character select. Seriously, what's up with that hazard toggle? It should have just been a fourth stage option, next to the Omega and Battlefield forms. The new squad strike is a really cool mode, but it takes too long to set up. It should have been treated like a normal stock smash mode, where you just pick multiple characters for each stock. It didn't need these extra menu options. Sorting and picking out spirit loadouts for the zillion spirit battles in the single player is also a little too slow and tedious for how many options you have to pick from. Also, have fun setting the music frequency. All of a series' stages share a track list, but each stage has its own song frequencies. There are 16 stages from the Mario series, with a list of over 90 songs to sort through, for every single stage. The song frequency slider gives way too much granular control, which isn't that bad by itself, but it takes too long to set a value. Then you have to do it for every song in this huge list. It makes setting up songs take way too long. Most people would have been happy with a coarser control, with maybe 4 or 5 frequency options like play never, rarely, sometimes, or play frequently. It's a great example of how settings meant for power users can degrade the experience for non-power users. In the end, these negatives are mostly just nitpicks. Smash Ultimate should be applauded for the good work it has done to fix its menus, but it's a reminder that no matter how good a game is, or how far it has come, there will always be more to do. Bad design. Deadly Premonition is janky. The gameplay is janky. The art style is janky. Sound design? Janky. Writing? Kinda fun, but still janky. And its interface? Super janky. Ugly type treatment, UI elements that clash with each other, low resolution art assets that get blown up into a blurry mess. Deadly Premonition's UI is full of inconsistency. Clashing UI elements can stick out in ways that take your audience out of the experience. A majority of the UI elements in Deadly Premonition are wildly different. We have the character's name in the upper left corner in a small, thin, serif typeface. Then in the lower right, we have this bold, italicized, and outlined font for the weapons. Above the weapons is this ammunition counter in a narrow typewriter font without any contrasting UI elements, outlines, or drop shadows to keep the text from blending into the background. For the dialogue, item description, and button interaction text, they use the same typewriter font from the ammunition counter, but now with a drop shadow for contrast. Why is that not on the ammunition counter? The deeper you dive, the weirder it gets. There are some rough looking bonus metal pop-ups for when you perform special actions like headshots or agent honor? Whatever that is. There are brackets placed around every key item name for reasons? Why do these button prompts at the bottom line up, but these don't? Why are these ugly character status bars overlapping the items folder? There's plenty of empty space beneath it. Some elements will use skeuomorphism like these office folders and crumpled paper, and other elements will just use black boxes, or nothing. Even similar UI elements will have different type styles. Both the items and mission lists submenus use an office folder as part of the design. That's all fine, but why is the style on the subheader type so different? Some items in those black boxes will have margins, and others just don't and look like you're highlighting something in a Word document. Over and over, Deadly Premonition shows what happens when a game refuses to commit to any one style. Good design Communication is so important in team strategy games, but lots of players mute voice chat, don't have a microphone on their system, can't understand what you're saying due to a language barrier, or just don't want to talk. So how can you take a game that relies on team communication and design it around the realities of voice chat? The ping tool in Apex Legends is brilliant. It's a simple way to take most of the tactical information you'd normally share over voice chat and cram it into one button press. It's not the first game to have a ping system, but they've made it more fully featured and easier to use than other games. You can tap the ping button while your aiming reticle is hovering over a location and it might tell your team to group up over there. Pinging on an enemy will highlight their last known location for the rest of your team. You can ping weapons, armor, upgrades, health, or any other pickups too. Your character in game will shout key information like the level of the armor or add-on and leave a marker on your teammate's HUD showing the item's location. Players can respond by pinging the HUD marker themselves to call dibs and keep the marker on screen, and can even easily thank whoever left the marker. Just like the Overwatch end of match endorsement system, it's a tiny psychological nudge that promotes better sportsmanship and team cohesion. No matter who your teammates are, their skill level in the game, or their hardware setup, they can help the team out with just one button press. The coolest part of the system might be how it gets around language barriers. By being a go-between for team communication, the game can take a ping sent from a Canadian player and localize it into Portuguese for their Brazilian teammate. Raw voice chat alone could never make communication so easy between teammates who speak different languages. The devs spent months playtesting the game with random names and no voice chat to emulate playing online with strangers. They iterated on the game with the lessons learned in those sessions and through a lot of hard work, came up with the friendliest team communication tool I've ever seen. There's a rule of thumb in design that you can tell you found a good solution if it solves a lot of problems at once. The ping system compensates for teammates missing or unwilling to use voice chat, helps communicate complex information, and solves a cross-cultural communication barrier. It is good design. Bad design. Most RPGs deal heavily with character progression and management. For most of them, that means fiddling with stats, equipment, and skills inside menus, from the start of the game to the end. Since you're in them so often, players notice when RPGs have rock-solid menus and navigation. Bad menu design sticks out and feels worse the more you have to use it. The first Mass Effect is amazing, but its menus and UI are not. It's not broken. It's not the worst interface I've ever seen, but aesthetically, it's bulky and bland. Functionally, it's inefficient. The Equipment screen is especially bad in the console versions of the game. It's not well organized and the screen space is used so inefficiently. Going from left to right, we have three core elements. The character preview, the equipped item with stat details, and your available inventory. Your items are listed in a single column, with just five pieces of equipment shown at once. There is no new marker. While inventory is divided by type, you can't sort

## Designing AI Allies - How Games Create Great Party Members and Companions ~ Design Doc
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tIze-mre0ss

I love games with unforgettable allies. That feeling you get when you team up with a new character gets me every time. Getting Orin to join permanently in Final Fantasy X, meeting a new partner in Paper Mario back when it was, you know, good, or Drogma from Skies of Arcadia.
Nope, never mind.
Oh, you're back. Great.
Oh. Okay.
In a lot of turn-based games, your party members were an extension of yourself.
You'd have full control over what they do on their turn.
In lots of more action-based games, however, you can't control your whole team at once, so you need to rely on AI to control your allies.
Designing and fine-tuning their automated behavior can make or break an entire game.
If they're too useful or powerful, you risk them playing the game for you.
If they're too weak or ineffective, they could become an unintentional liability, or you might forget that they're even there.
In a perfect world, these characters should feel like they make a real contribution without stealing the fun from the player.
That's easy to say, but clearly there are pitfalls everywhere.
Let's look at how some games approach AI companion design successfully and unsuccessfully,
and talk about how both the mechanics and the story of a game can influence AI design.
There's an idea in psychology called loss aversion that says that losing something feels more negative than gaining it feels positive.
One way to design an AI around loss aversion is instead of depending on a character and being disappointed if they fail to help,
switch it up and have an AI character occasionally give out bonuses.
Just framing the player's expectations differently can make them happier, even if they're getting the same benefits on average either way.
The Palicos of Monster Hunter World are a good example of how to design around loss aversion.
Palicos are great at distracting monsters and creating opportunities during fights.
They don't do much damage, but they make up for it in utility and customization.
They can be equipped with status-inflicting weapons and special Palico tools that can heal you, give you buffs, set up traps, or they can even steal monster materials.
They will use these skills on their own, but you can command them manually if you want to.
There's no major penalty if they run out of health either. They have autonomy without being a liability.
Some Palico equipment loadouts are better than others, but they all provide at least some benefit, but never so much that they make the monster hunting at the core of the game too easy.
If Monster Hunter framed Palicos as allies that did a major part of the monster hunting, the same behaviors would feel disappointing.
But since they're more of a companion that gives out bonuses, and they only show up when you don't have many actual players in your party, they feel like good partners.
They're great during the beginning of the game while you figure out the ropes, and they don't get in the way of high-end monster hunting.
And above all, it's a cat. It's adorable. Don't overthink it.
There's a murky middle ground for AI design that you can see in Kingdom Hearts.
One of the running jokes with Kingdom Hearts 1 and 2 was that Donald and Goofy were the poster boys for useless companions.
I revisited Kingdom Hearts 1, and I was surprised in the early game. They actually did more than I ever gave them credit for.
They'll automatically attack enemies, using offensive and support skills to help you out.
You can also use the triangle button to send them after a specific target that you're locked onto.
They do well enough against the fodder in the early game, but once tougher enemies and bosses come into the picture, they just can't keep up.
Unlike the Palicos, Donald, Goofy, and the various guest party members don't create many opportunities for you during fights.
They can't really evade or block attacks well, they waste MP by whiffing attacks, and they'll take slivers away from the enemy's health while Sora takes out huge chunks with each hit.
They don't know how to protect themselves, and will quickly burn through any items you give them.
When they're not doing chip damage or wasting items, they're probably unconscious.
They end up being much more useful if you customize their skills and behaviors to focus on support skills like MP Gift and Cure.
It's nice that the game is flexible enough to let you do that, but it's a little disappointing to have to override some bad AI if you want Donald and Goofy to be as useful as I think the game intended them to be.
Kingdom Hearts 2 tried to make them more useful in combat with the limits and drive forms that require your party members to perform.
And it helps a bit, but they still can't do that much on their own.
They also took out most of the support abilities and the AI control, so even going back to the strategies you used in Kingdom Hearts 1 isn't as effective anymore.
The AI feels like wasted potential, requiring too much hand-holding to be effective, but they're not so useless as to break the game.
Luckily, Kingdom Hearts 3 fixes a lot of the series' AI problems.
Your party members will do decent damage this time.
There are new team combo finishers that trigger if they're nearby.
The game has lots of customization options like Kingdom Hearts 1, and special limit commands like Kingdom Hearts 2.
Your party feels more complete, strategically anyway.
Ally design can also become a problem if you don't properly frame what the AI members should be responsible for.
In Star Fox Assault, there's a disconnect between what the game says the AI characters are there for, and what the game actually does with them.
Star Fox is supposed to be a team of space mercenaries, emphasis on team, but it's mostly just a Fox McCloud show.
Let's use the third mission of Star Fox Assault as an example.
In this all-range map, you have to infiltrate a space station to take out a number of enemy spawners.
While you look for them, enemy ships will periodically spawn outside of the station.
As more ships appear, a meter will fill up, and if it maxes out, the mission will fail.
Your teammates will either help you on foot in the station, or fend off the enemies outside in Arwings.
Heh, just kidding. They're just flying around in circles taking random potshots.
Or firing at me!
You'll have to go outside yourself to clear the area before the meter maxes out.
Your ally on the ground can actually hold their own, kinda like an auto-turret, but they'll only stay within a very small space.
Scripted events will show your wingmates being useful, but the second they're needed in the actual game, it turns out they're really just there for show.
The framing of the role of your wingmates is confusing, and makes the situation feel like a missed opportunity.
Ace Combat 7 has exactly the same problem, actually, but in every mission.
The series gives you wingmates every game, and Ace Combat 5 even lets you guide their behavior.
Ace Combat 7, however, has teammates that take random shots at random targets, and you have no way of making them do anything else.
Very, very rarely will your wingmates take out any of the mission-critical targets marked in red.
Instead, you might see them pick off a non-critical target once in a while. Or maybe just nothing.
It's the same problem as Star Fox, but it's a strange regression for a series that had more or less fixed the problem in an earlier game.
If this makes you think that maybe you know better than the AI programmers, and you should just make the AI yourself, you should try Final Fantasy XII.
The gambit system in FFXII lets you program exactly the steps, or gambits, that your AI party members will take in battle, in a kind of Lego brick sort of way.
For example, you can set a gambit to have a character cast healing spells whenever someone's HP drops below a set threshold, or automatically cast haste on the party whenever you can't.
More advanced and specific conditions for gambits can be found in shops as the game progresses.
You also have to consider the priorities of your gambits, placing more situational instructions at the top, and common ones at the bottom.
If you have attacking nearby enemies as a top priority, the other gambits will never be used.
It's not that far off in concept from what an actual AI programmer might code, but this way you feel like you're in control if the AI screws something up.
Even though the gambit system needs micromanaging like in Kingdom Hearts, the framing is completely different.
Managing gambits is a huge part of the game, so it's not as frustrating as the micromanaging was in Kingdom Hearts.
Players expect it, so they're okay with putting in the time.
The idea of what a player expects a character to do is pretty central to AI design, but an AI's expectations can also overlap with a game's story.
The narrative of a game can make an AI character behave unexpectedly, but there is a way to do it that won't frustrate players as much.
God of War 4's story is all about the father-son relationship between Kratos and Atreus.
The developers at Santa Monica designed Atreus to always feel like he was contributing during combat.
He can shoot arrows and summon creatures on your command with a single button.
He'll follow up on your attacks when he's nearby, and he can distract and stun enemies and open them up for you.
You don't have to micromanage him beyond equipping stat-boosting gear and occasionally saving him when he gets caught by an enemy.
Atreus also acts as your hint guide and helps you solve puzzles.
He's not treated like an escort character, but the game does turn him into a liability in combat to fit with some of the story beats.
In a later section of the game, Atreus won't always listen to your commands and will recklessly lead you into bad situations.
He'll even start

## The Evolution of Roguelike Design - How Rogue led to FTL, Spelunky, and So Many More ~ Design Doc
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uM588ci-sMQ

It's hard to find a genre more hotly debated than roguelikes. Whether or not a game counts as a roguelike can be debated for hours. Now I'm not about to dive into roguelikes versus roguelites, but for me, the more interesting question is what makes the genre so adaptable? The fact that so many unique styles of games are arguably roguelikes means there are some interesting things going on in their design. We've watched a flood of roguelikes get released over the past 10 years that all feel very different, but they still rhyme. So what is it about the design of roguelikes that can adapt to so many different settings and play styles? And how have the most popular games over time taken that roguelike core and evolved it into something fresh and new? Today, let's talk about the design of roguelikes and why they're such a hotbed for modern game design experimentation. So what is a roguelike? It's definitely this, and this, but it could also be this, or this, or this. The term roguelike comes from old Usenet discussion boards where people search for games that were similar to Rogue. Rogue was created in 1980 by Glenn Wickman, Michael Toy, and Ken Arnold, and released at first for Unix mainframes, then adapted for home computers. It wasn't the first game that we might today call a roguelike, but it became very popular. Rogue was the standard, and so the other games imitating it were called roguelikes. Over the next few decades, different offshoots like the Mystery Dungeon games and Linley's Dungeon Crawl would borrow tons of elements from Rogue, refining systems and slowly morphing what a roguelike could be. To try to nail down what exactly a roguelike was, a group of developers came together in 2008 at the International Roguelike Development Conference in Berlin to create a checklist of eight must-haves for any pure roguelike. First, random dungeon generation. The game should randomly put together dungeons from scratch or from custom prefabricated pieces. Second, permadeath. No checkpoints. Your actions could have deadly consequences, so you better keep an eye out for trouble. Third, turn-based gameplay. The world only takes action when you do. Step for step, attack for attack. You can plan your next move for as long as you like. Fourth, non-modal gameplay. This just means that you have every action available to you from the start of the game, and there aren't any different modes you enter while you're playing. It contrasts with a metroidvania-style system that grants new abilities as you play the game. In a pure roguelike, you should be able to go wherever you want and interact with everything you see. Fifth, emergent gameplay. The world operates under certain rules, like say, flammability, fatigue, health limits, poison, and dozens of other mechanics. The rules apply to the world and its characters just as much as they apply to you. Sixth, limited resources. You have a certain amount of health, stamina, time, steps, or other resources. Manage them well to stay alive for as long as you can. Seventh, hack and slash gameplay. This one's pretty specific. In a traditional roguelike, you will be fighting through waves of enemies and clearing dungeon floors. Eighth, mystery items. The things you come across on your journey might have special properties, but you might not have any idea what they'll do. Even if you've seen the same item before, item properties can change in a new life. This list of eight high-value key factors is called the Berlin Interpretation of Roguelikes. I think it's a little limiting, but at least we can use that as a definition for the most vanilla roguelike. And it's a great starting point for talking about how games have tweaked the basic design into all the different flavors of roguelike-inspired games that exist today. Different combos of the eight elements of the Berlin Interpretation play off of each other incredibly well and help create the feel of a roguelike. Mystery items and random dungeon generation make each new session a unique experience. Turn-based and non-modal gameplay make you feel like you're driving the game's outcome at your own pace, rather than waiting for the game to unlock something to let you proceed or being rushed into making a hasty decision. Limited resources and permadeath raise the stakes. Even though you can just start a new life, you don't get the same resources every time. Every play session becomes something worth preserving. But the most important combo of them all might be random dungeon generation and permadeath. These combine to make run-based gameplay, which is the very heart of the roguelike, the common denominator between almost all the games with that roguelike feel. Run-based gameplay is a way to make a game that feels surprising and fair, rewarding and replayable. From a familiar set of base elements, it creates unexpected new experiences. It rewards understanding systems instead of memorizing and klutzing your way through the same encounters over and over. These game design combos are kind of like chords in music. The same chord can be in dozens of hit songs, each of them with their own feel, but they all use the same basic tool to get there. They're all unique paths using the same stepping stone. It's maybe what's a little strange about the Berlin Interpretation. I don't think that it's useful to stick to a rigid definition. It's helpful when you want to study the elements of a design, but sticking to it too closely will just get you cookie-cutter reskins of classics. If you start thinking of a roguelike as a mosaic of elements instead of a monolith, you open dozens of new possibilities and really good spinoff games that still have a core that's recognizable as inspired by classic roguelike design. So let's see what shows up if we start tinkering with the Berlin Interpretation a bit. Okay, starting with the strict Berlin Interpretation, we've got Rogue. Let's start by tweaking one of the low-value components. There's no reason we have to stick with ASCII graphics. Put a coat of paint on everything and give your imagination a break by showing actual sprites. Done. You've discovered Dungeon Crawler's Stone Soup or Dungeons of Dredmor. They're exactly as deep mechanically, but way easier for a beginner to understand what's going on without thumbing through a manual every two seconds. Now let's start changing some of the high-value components. What if we start with that turn-based gameplay rule? The game doesn't have to let you think about your decisions forever. Real-time combat can still reward understanding the systems that the game has in place. It can still be very replayable and the stakes can be just as high, but you just won't have as long to sit there and think through your actions. That sounds an awful lot like Binding of Isaac or Enter the Gungeon to me. They're roguelike experiences wrapped around a much more action-heavy combat system, but when you make a run in either of those games, it's just as compelling for all the same reasons as a run in Rogue or NetHack. While we're here swapping out turn-based gameplay, we could get even weirder with it. Instead of taking out turns entirely, maybe we could use a system that gives them a new meaning. What if the turns were musical beats instead? It would keep the same move-for-move structure that most roguelikes have, but you still have to think quickly to be effective. Now you've made Crypt of the Necrodancer. You do have to compensate for some of these tweaks though. Necrodancer has to tone down the difficulty a bit because you have less time to plan. If it kept the same level of difficulty as a traditional roguelike, it would feel far too punishing. It's hard to think through all the complicated systems when you're busy keeping the beat. Necrodancer still lets you crank up the difficulty to ridiculous levels, but the base game is more forgiving. The game morphs into a roguelike that rewards feel, improvisation, reaction, and flow. The game's runs are shorter too, to help keep a mistake from ruining too much of your time. Also, tying a run to the end of a level's song is a smart and natural way to force players to keep moving throughout the level before time expires. And Necrodancer has a killer soundtrack. Very few roguelikes tie their soundtrack to gameplay, so that's another way to make the game unique and deeply memorable. Okay, let's change up random dungeon generation. What if instead of a literal set of rooms and corridors, we have a branching path of encounters instead, and keep that real-time combat around too? That sounds like FTL to me. The weapons and systems you build up over time are very Rogue-inspired. Permadeath is a constant threat, and the emergent gameplay rules are in full effect with all the different ways you can take out enemy ships, through boarding their ship and taking it over, setting the ship on fire, destroying their oxygen supply, mind controlling their crew and having them fight each other, or just blasting them to bits. FTL abstracts the idea of a dungeon from a series of rooms to a series of encounters, but it absolutely nails run-based gameplay, and still very much feels like a roguelike. Let's go back to classic random dungeon generation and now look at the permadeath wedge. One of the most popular tweaks has been in relaxing the permadeath restriction. Permadeath is a vital piece of the core of the roguelike feel, but progression is really satisfying in games. People like to change and improve over time. Making each run feel important and worth preserving relies heavily on permadeath, so we can't just swap it out entirely. But what if you could keep just a little piece of yourself between runs? Now you've got Dead Cells and Rogue Legacy, among lots of others. Dead Cells and Rogue Legacy don't just implement this mechanically, they're both narratively themed around

## The Decline of SSX ~ Design Doc
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=edWW_GXQukk

Back in the early 2000s, most people latched onto Tony Hawk for their extreme sports fix, but I was more about snowboarding. And what's the first game you think of when you think snowboarding? That's right, Snowboard Kids. But today we'll talk about SSX. It's no Snowboard Kids, but it's still pretty alright. Atlas, make a new Snowboard Kids. No, not that one. The SSX series is iconic, a fantastic blend of outlandish tracks, personalities, fast-paced arcade racing, and Tony Hawk-style tricks. And as a series, it's… kinda dead. There hasn't been any sign of a new SSX title after the polarizing 2012 reboot. It may be a long time before we have any hope of EA rekindling SSX, but I think the series is too good to be forgotten. So today, I want to go over SSX Tricky, SSX 3, SSX On Tour, and SSX 2012 to rediscover what made it a beloved series and how it faded away. Oh, and here I'll quick mention the original SSX and the Wii-exclusive SSX Blur. Blur was a weird motion controls experiment that reused tons of SSX 3 and On Tour content, and didn't work too well. The original SSX was fine, but Tricky is a direct upgrade, and where the series first hit its stride. Just play Tricky if you're going to go that far back. So, let's get tricky. SSX Tricky is famous for its goofy, funky 70s tone mixed in with late 90s extreme sports and as many run DMC samples as they could fit. Well, one sample, but it's everywhere. The game is stylish and energetic, with an over-the-top cast including red-headed disco nerds, thuggish rednecks, unhinged masochists, adrenaline junkies, and of course, who could forget, Ansem from Kingdom Hearts 1. Synchronicity. Our destinies are intertwined. The final darkness is nigh. Cap it off with Rozelle on the mic as the announcer and you get a game that's just oozing with personality. The characters matter, not just for the personality they inject into the game, but they have pre-existing relationships with each other. These are more than just part of their backstory. They influence how aggressive the AI will be. You can knock down other characters to quickly fill your boost meter, but it's a risk in the long run as they'll get more aggressive towards you in later races. Tricky's track design is filled with personality too. Crashing through buildings in Mercury City, treacherous ice caves in Alaska, the pinball layout and circuit structure of Tokyo Megaplex. Each of the 10 tracks have a distinct feel, which I love. SSX Tricky, and really the series in general, focuses its gameplay on impossible tricks and huge air. This is where the Uber Trick system comes into play. Landing tricks does more than just rack up points. The more complicated the trick, the more boost you build. Filling the boost meter to the top grants time-limited access to the series' trademark Uber Tricks, where your character becomes a snowboard wizard. The tricks are risky and take time to perform, but with each Uber you land, you're rewarded with tons of points and boost meter. Performing six Uber Tricks in the same run will grant infinite boosts for the rest of the course. Tying boosts to these Uber Tricks is an elegant way to make sure the trick system is not just for trick events. It's still an important part of the game's race events. It rewards taking risks, gives reason to learn the course and plan your run, and the graphical and audio treatment make it just viscerally satisfying to land all these impossible tricks back to back to back. I love Tricky, but there was still room to improve. The board handling is fine, but not that precise. Grinding on rails is tougher than it should be with some awkward hit detection. The game isn't set up to let you land a specific trick that easily, which is only really a problem in the trick book challenges that unlock costumes and the best board in the game. Uber Tricks are also a little awkward because of how the controls overlap with the grab trick modifiers, which puts a weird limit on some of your trick options. But Tricky overall holds up very well for its age. SSX3 came out in 2003, two years after the release of Tricky. While Tricky was a refinement of the original, SSX3 was more of a true sequel. The trick system was expanded and refined. They fixed Tricky's air control problems. The rails got a complete overhaul with rail-based Uber Tricks and handstands. And they fixed the hit detection. SSX3 also added nose and tail presses. They make up the core of a new combo system, which feels lifted right out of Tony Hawk. You store bonus points into a combo counter as you perform trick after trick without wiping out. You only have a few seconds to keep the combo going, so stringing together air tricks, rail tricks, and presses is key to beating trick challenges this time. The Uber Trick system returns with a few tweaks. There are now three tiers of Uber. As you land more Uber Tricks, you will unlock new tiers of tricks that you can perform that run. Land five tricks from the second tier and you'll get infinite boost for a little while. The Uber Tricks were also tweaked. Instead of a long animation, Ubers act more like better but slower grabs, racking up more points the longer you hold them. The trick system overhaul was balanced with the game's new longer courses in mind. Each course is connected in an open mountain layout. Instead of going to single events in isolated courses, tracks and events are divided among three peaks. Complete race and trick events to eventually go toe-to-toe with the boss rival of the peak and unlock the next one. Each peak branches out into a handful of tracks. Every track segues into small intermission hub areas where you organically choose which event you want to start next. The open mountain is a promising idea. It gives some nice natural opportunities for downtime between races, and there are a few fun challenges scattered across the mountain. It's especially good on your first few runs as you're acclimatizing to the game, but the idea starts to buckle under the weight of sticking to the open mountain premise. It adds an extra step to starting events, which gets a bit old before long. The connected mountain also limits what you can do with the course variety. There's nothing as creative as the Tokyo Megaplex to pass through, and it'd be disorienting if there was. The tracks that do exist, to their credit, are great, but I don't believe they're on average as memorable as the ones in Tricky. You'll see lots of standard slopes and harsh tundras. Even the more distinct city and forest courses don't stand out quite as much as the most memorable Tricky courses. You won't see anything quite like Aloha Ice Jam, for example. Like the tracks, the characters in 3 have also been toned down a bit. They took out most of the aggression system. Only the pre-designated rivals of each peak will ever try to knock you down, usually on the final run. Knocking the AI down will aggro them in that event. Don't worry about it, though. The courses are more spread out, so you'll hardly see your opponents anyway, and they'll completely forget about your shoving match by the next race. The personality and voice lines are still there, but it's a little more muted than before. Where Tricky is funky and over-the-top, SSX3 is cool, laid-back, and ambient. Taking Rozelle's place as the announcer this time is DJ Atomica, who provides smoother commentary during intermissions between events. We're back with EA Radio Big. SSX3 is a fully realized, amazing snowboarding experience. It brought over the most important parts of Tricky, and refined some of the sketchier bits. It's probably the best in the series, but it just felt a little more muted than its predecessor. EA might have carved off a few too many edges. Two years after SSX3 came SSX On Tour, which brought some important tweaks. And skis, but no one cares about skis. The first change was to the game's aesthetic. The vibrant funk and cool ambience is gone, and in its place is a sketchy punk look. These menus filled with trapper-keeper doodles are pretty fun, actually, but the personality disappears when you meet the cast. The character designs have been greatly toned down, and the characters are only playable in quick play. The main mode is reserved for everyone's favorite fountain of personality, a custom avatar. And what's better than racing as your self-insert custom avatar? Racing against other randomized avatars! Personality! The old SSX cast will show up in basic title cards before you face them in easy rival events, but they have almost no personality. The old cast is barely any different from the avatars. The tracks in On Tour have the same open mountain feel as SSX3, but with its problems magnified. You ride down mostly standard slopes and backcountry tracks with small distinct features placed here and there. It's still cool to run down an entire mountain, but these tracks blend together even worse than last time. The samey courses aren't helped by the game's new rank-based progression system. Instead of completing events linearly, On Tour's campaign has you climb up a rankings board to become number one in the SSX Tour. You complete events and challenges to gain hype, raise your rank, and unlock more events. On paper it's an interesting new approach to progression, but in practice you'll play the same courses over and over to try to eke out enough hype to get to the next tier of events. The difficulty curve ramps up slowly, and the major race and trick events can take a long time to

## Good Design, Bad Design Vol. 4 - The Best and Worst of Video Game Graphic Design ~ Design Doc
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5mjQl3En6zQ

Welcome back to another installment of Good Design, Bad Design, where we look at how games approach graphic design. While there's a lot of overlap between the two, good graphic design isn't exactly the same as good art. Good graphic design covers things like menus, UI, camera work, color choice, font choice, animation, character design, the presentation of information. We have six more examples today, and while some of these examples get into concepts that are connected to each other, they aren't strictly paired up. Also, remember that beautiful games can have bad graphic design, and vice versa. Games with bad graphic design aren't necessarily bad games, but good graphic design can help make a good game into a great one. Okay, let's begin. Good Design It's been years since we had a flood of game series making the jump from 2D to 3D, but it's easy to forget how important that period of gaming history was. So much of what we think of as standard in today's games was first designed in that era. There are a select few games that stand out as the best of the best in 2D to 3D conversion, Mario 64, Ocarina of Time, and I'd argue Metroid Prime belongs right next to them. The beauty of Metroid Prime's 3D adaptation is not just that it kept the classic structure and exploration intact, it's in how it kept the same atmosphere and sense of isolation that makes up Metroid's identity. To maintain the atmosphere, the designers at Retro Studios had to make some big changes. 3D could let them make a stronger connection between the player and Samus, but they would need to overhaul how the game was presented. They had to put the player into Samus' shoes, or more accurately, her head. Metroid Prime's helmet HUD is more immersive than the HUD of the 2D Metroid games. It still shows all the same info from the 2D games, energy meters, missile ammunition, and maps, but now it adds new elements like lock-on indicators, hazard meters, weapons, visors, and radar. Elements that feel like what Samus would actually use, building that information right into her visor. The new visor framing lets the designers add some interesting mechanics too. After taking some... weird input from Miyamoto, Retro added things like the X-ray and thermal filters, and then used them for puzzle solving. The filters wouldn't have made sense without the first-person view and visor framing, but they also added another layer to the environments and the feeling of a more realistic space for Samus to travel through. The visor scanner was new too, and gave a nice new way to show optional gameplay tips and storytelling. There are so many other little touches that strengthen the connection between the player and the character. Lots of these techniques are common now, but for the time it was a real step forward in immersion. Flashes of light will reveal the reflection of Samus' eyes, the way the helmet slightly shifts as you look around, the alien splatter from exploding enemies, the electrical interference from taking damage, the raindrops that increase in frequency as you look up in the rain. The line between the player and Samus is blurred, done as realistically as they could with the hardware of the day, and the change in perspective immerses Metroid Prime's players in the same atmosphere and sense of isolation that made the series a classic in the first place.
Bad Design
So, Hover was a thing. Oh, I'm sorry.
Hover Revolt of Gamers.
Hover is a multiplayer-focused open-world parkour game that was pitched as a spiritual successor to Jet Set Radio.
It's got the premise, art style, and music to match, but the UI design is...
Hover's UI design is impractical and sloppy. There are big, sweeping problems with almost every element in your HUD.
The objective list only shows three and a half objectives, and you can't choose which objectives to track like in, say, Borderlands or most other quest-driven games.
There's a Crazy Taxi-style waypoint arrow that points towards either your next objective or the nearest quest giver.
And it can flip-flop between the two at a moment's notice, and there's no way to lock it to an objective or waypoint.
There are things like the chat log and player list that don't need to be on screen all the time, but they are.
All of these text boxes aren't scrollable without pausing the game, and it's pretty clunky to take up screen space all the time just to see the last thing someone said.
Then there's the area map that's hands-down one of the worst maps I've ever seen. Just look at it. There's no detail.
Only a few of the landmarks are shown with these city walls at the edge of the map and these two highway roads.
These other signs don't really tell you anything, and with the world's vertical design, it's hard to tell where the quest givers actually are.
Inside each UI element is another problem. Hover uses a tiny, crowded font in different backgrounds that make the game's text difficult to read.
Here's a quick typography lesson. There are three main kinds of spacing.
There's kerning, the spacing between a pair of letters. There's tracking, which is the letter spacing applied evenly to a group of letters.
And there's leading, which is the vertical spacing between lines of text.
A graphic designer can adjust these properties for different stylistic effects, and it's a subtle part of what makes good and readable typography.
But you can royally screw it up, too. Hover's text tracking and leading are both uncomfortably close.
The font they use throughout the game has some weird design choices for some of the letter shapes.
The R and S are tiny. The O, A, and even G could easily be mistaken for each other.
The cramped typeface doesn't match well with the game's tone and was clearly designed around the PC.
The type is the same on the console versions, where there have been tons of complaints about how small the type is, especially on the Switch.
The header typefaces in the other UI elements also have sloppy typesetting and placement.
The hard-to-read font is then put on a semi-transparent background, which makes it even harder to read, especially when it covers the glowing game environments.
Yes, you can get used to the interface, but one of the points of good design is to get information to someone easily.
Hover's UI makes it tougher to play the game, and there's no good reason that that should be the case.
But even if Hover has some major problems, at least it gave the world a couple new Hideki Naganuma tracks.
Ah, maybe Hover's not so bad. Ugh, never mind.
Good Design
Journey was a major influence for me wanting to study graphic design.
It's masterful in its minimalistic storytelling, and that minimalism bleeds into all of Journey's design.
Journey has no traditional UI, but there's one piece that helps drive its players through the game in a way that works perfectly with its narrative.
I'm talking about the scarf. Love that scarf.
Hidden throughout Journey are these ancient glyphs that when collected, magically transform into an elegant red and orange scarf.
The scarf pattern represents energy that allows you to jump.
As you jump, your energy depletes and is only refilled by touching other pieces of fabric, like these bridges, cloth creatures, or another player.
As you go through the game and find more of these symbols, the scarf expands and so does your energy.
Find enough symbols and you're basically able to fly.
You don't actually need a long scarf to finish Journey, but it gorgeously flows in the wind and the jump feels so empowering.
The scarf is valuable for the mechanics it provides, but Journey is a game about meeting random people and helping each other through the experience.
Without words or numbers or titles, the scarf becomes a symbol for a player's experience in the game.
Jumping could have just been tied to a stamina or MP bar in the corner, but by making it part of your character, it connects the player to the narrative and is a starting point for random players online to form a bond with each other.
The Hidden Glyphs gives you a reason to explore and to cooperate, with the more experienced players guiding newer ones through the glyphs, all just for a bigger scarf.
Without words and without a traditional interface, Journey's designers give an item that feels like a gift and a reward.
The presentation of Journey's scarf is a lovely design and is part of the foundation of an ambitious, wordless narrative.
Bad Design
Video games have a quirk that makes them trickier to design.
The fun of a game often comes from overcoming a challenge, but for single player games, a game designer has to design both the problem and the solution.
They create the villain and the hero, the burning hospital and the fire hose.
Wait, this makes game design sound like an extortion racket.
Huh.
Anyway, the tricky part is in the balance.
If the problem overwhelms the tools used to solve it, the game becomes frustrating.
If the solution is overpowered, the game can become boring.
It's easy to think of something like an overpowered weapon or a broken magic spell that can upset the balance of a game, but it's not just the problem for systems based around numbers.
Overpowered tools can also compromise other elements of a game's design, like its UI and art direction.
A perfect example of this shows up with Detective Vision in Batman Arkham Asylum.
Detective Vision is a visual filter that lets players get a clear view of the environment, highlighting the location and status of enemies and key interactables through walls.
It's incredibly useful.
In fact, I'd argue that it's almost too useful.
There are no gameplay downsides to flipping it on, and there's nothing that keeps you from using it all the time.
Many players develop a reliance on the tool because without it, they feel blind.
Without it, enemies and objects are so much harder to see and track.
Players rarely turn the mode off in order to

## The Design of Octopath Traveler ~ Design Doc
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tuKHsssldTE

Octopath Traveler had one of the best teasers I've ever seen. It showed a vision for how to refresh the old Square RPG style into a modern context. But it was just a teaser. It didn't guarantee that the actual game would deliver on that vision. Octopath Traveler is stunning on its surface. It's got a great look, a beautiful soundtrack, and fun gameplay. But it has structural problems, especially in its story that take off some of the shine. It's a game whose quality is divided over the biggest two aspects of any JRPG, the game mechanics and the storytelling. Let's talk about the design of Octopath Traveler through its RPG mechanics and its storytelling and explore what went right and what went wrong. Octopath Traveler is an RPG dense in game mechanics. It's got tons of equipment, Final Fantasy-style character jobs, SMT-style elemental and attack type weaknesses, visible turn orders like Final Fantasy X, and BP, which works a lot like the Brave system in Bravely Default. They all combine to make a very strategic battle experience. The combat is all focused around weaknesses. You'll want to create a team with the right jobs to have a wide range of elemental and physical attack options. Use every type of attack you can to discover an enemy's weaknesses, then use that knowledge to whittle their guard down to zero, which breaks your opponent and forces them to skip some of their turns. This basic strategy works well to take care of normal enemies quickly, but boss fights especially rely on you discovering and targeting weaknesses. The game's bosses are often very resilient, especially if you're a bit underleveled, and they can easily take out one or several of your party members if you're too cavalier about how you fight. The battle system is rich with tactical options and rewards flexibility and adaptation, but there's a problem. If you've found the right set of weaknesses and are exploiting them fully, the boss might not get many moves against you. You feel pretty safe, almost like you've solved the puzzle, but the bosses tend to be damage sponges, and you're left fighting for another ten minutes to take them down. Some people like endurance boss fights like that, but I don't think Octopath's bosses feel like a marathon fight for survival like some of the best long boss fights do. Later boss fights do switch up their weaknesses mid-fight, and that can add a little tension, but it's not complicated to adapt to it, and it doesn't actually change the combat loop much. Even so, the combat of Octopath is very nice, and one of the best parts of the game. Outside of combat, I love the idea of Octopath's out-of-battle actions. Each character in your active party can do something specific, called a path action, to almost every NPC in the game. You can beat them up, charm them into helping you in battle, press them for more information, or just rob them blind. Two of your party members might have the same type of action, but one may have the risky or rogue version, and one may have the less risky noble version of the action. With more risk, you can reap greater rewards, but you can also go too far and alienate everyone in town if, say, you're caught stealing too many times. The range of things your party can do in towns makes your party composition actually important outside of battle. Do you bring your underleveled apothecary? He might not be the strongest member of the team, but he can talk to the townspeople and get some free information. Do you double up your hunter and warrior? They're great in fights, but they both have the same path action type, which forces you to go without some of your options if you're too far from a tavern to swap out party members. There's one easy decision at least. You always want the thief. Sorry, Tressa. There's just so much stuff to steal. Merchants? Yoink. Sickly Kid? Yoink. Sickly Kid's mom? Yoink. That medicine wasn't working anyway. Octopath has wonderful mechanics, even if they're not perfect. The battle system is deep and fun, and the path action system makes your party feel like it's dealing with NPCs in their own personal style. But RPGs aren't all about mechanics. I feel the core of an RPG is the story it tells, and the story of Octopath Traveler could be told better. Oh, and here's your spoiler warning. Minor early and mid-game spoilers ahead. Nothing major, you'll be fine. Your characters are traveling through the world of Orsterra, which is quite pretty. Unique and interesting biomes are all over the place, and the wilds flow fairly well, from town to town, key location to key location. I should be clear. The physical world is well put together. The societal setup for the world is not. Each location is a pretty standard JRPG town that specializes in one thing, and one thing only. It's even in their name. Cobblestone. Saint's Bridge. Noble Court. Boulderfall. Sunshade. Still Snow. Merchant Port. Forest Zone. I like Church Sylvania. But the locations aren't tied together very well into a cohesive world. The towns don't seem to interact that much. Even within the same town, you don't feel a strong connection with the rest of the game. When two of the game's chapters happen in the same place, you're not interacting with the same NPCs, you're not dealing with similar or even related goals, and you're going to different locations in and around the area. The chapters might as well be in two different towns. Orsterra's locations feel vibrant at first, but that worldbuilding momentum gets tossed aside in every new chapter, and eventually makes the locations feel a bit cookie-cutter. While traveling in Orsterra, you'll meet eight people and take them through eight different paths, or individual stories. Each character is focused on their own story, traveling from town to town seeking purpose, information, freedom, adventure, or vengeance. On paper, it's a good idea. There isn't one main character among the eight, really. Each is equally important. You get to pick what character you start as, and then travel around collecting the others at your own pace. You don't even need to get everyone. But in practice, the freedom of the game's narrative comes at a cost. There is nothing to tie these eight threads together. Each character is an island unto themselves. Instead of a critical plot thread with a central goal, the game tells eight equally important story arcs, chopped up and served one part at a time. There are no interweaving plot lines, and worse than that, there pretty much can't be any. Any one chapter can only be sure that you've seen the previous chapter of the same character. It knows nothing about the state of the world or your other party members. They don't even show up in the cutscenes. It's almost like the eight characters are just in each other's chapters as a favor, like helping them move or something. Let's say you're in the middle of Therion's story. He's a thief, and has to steal several powerful artifacts for a wealthy, shady family in order to regain his freedom. In any other RPG, the rest of your party might have something to say about his situation. Cyrus, the world-class mage scholar, might dive into the mysteries of the artifacts. Olberic, the steadfast knight, might grouse about the dishonor of their circumstances. But not in Octopath. Everyone else is just hanging around, somewhere off-screen while the cutscenes are happening. You'll sometimes get a chance to hear a party member and the starring character talk for a second after a cutscene ends. They might touch on some character moments, but they don't reference events from other characters' chapters, and they never change the course of the current plot. They're nothing but flavor text, and they're easy to miss. If you don't have the right people in your party, or even if you just didn't see the prompt in the top corner of the screen, you'll skip over the scene entirely. It doesn't even have something like the Fire Emblem support conversation system, where the party banter might have told a story that progressed over time. Instead, the dialogue plays the same whether Alphen is still a bright-eyed optimist or if he's been betrayed a couple of times. Primrose will say the same thing no matter if she's in her Chapter 1 or her Chapter 4. It's funny, the screen even goes into a weird darkened scene with spotlights when they start talking, kinda like they're in a stage play for a minute. It makes the conversation feel even more detached from the game world. When it's done, the game fades back in and you continue like nothing happened. The characters end up feeling a little static because they are static, left without an arc outside of their personal plot advancement zone. Within each scene, Octopath's writing is...passable. JRPGs are notorious for wildly varying story quality, and the content of Octopath's story is certainly not the worst I've ever played. A lot of the character arcs are very standard RPG tropes, but that's fine. Cartoonish villains are thwarted by cartoonish heroes, with an occasional detour to some more nuanced and surprisingly dark chapters. Thanks to the Inquirer and Scrutinized Path actions, there is a ton of backstory you can read about most of the NPCs in the game. They all have a little blurb about how they relate to the other people in town. It does help bring the world to life to a certain extent, and some of the side quests make use of it. But the writing can get fairly long-winded. The voice acting is...fine. The actors do an okay job with the script they're given, but sometimes that script is the worst, most noticeably with Honnit. Tis not the hunt that concerneth me. Thou intendest to stop and off somewhere along the way. The voice actress is doing fine, but listening to Honnit's terrible fake old English dialect makes me

## Kart Racers - Designing Fun for Everyone ~ Design Doc
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=P8S176RmRJg

Man, there are so many kart racers. M&M's Kart Racing, South Park Rally, Garfield Kart, that Shrek one, and all the good ones. Kart racers have an absolutely enormous appeal. Everyone from young kids, casual players, adults who rarely play games, veteran players, or speedrunners, they cover practically every segment of the gaming audience. It's not by accident either. It's a product of their design. Let's dissect some of the parts that make up a kart racer, course design, driving mechanics, and item design, and see how different games create a layered kart racing experience that appeals to just about everybody. First up, course design. For a kart racer to be appealing, players of all skill levels need to be doing something more than just turn now, turn now, accelerate, now turn some more. More advanced players spend time thinking about things like race lines, item strategy, positioning, that kind of thing. For total newcomers though, the easiest way that a kart racer can grab a player's attention is through colorful and mind-bending courses. Modern Mario Kart is great at using the track theme to create interesting track layouts. To design a great track, you can't just create a quick circuit with a few turns and call it a day. The best tracks thrive on a healthy mix of set pieces and distinct themes that make the track memorable, to see and to play. The work of the track designers shows up in courses like Daisy Cruiser, where you blaze through the decks of a cruise liner while avoiding tables that slide around as the ship rocks back and forth. Coconut Mall, where you're bouncing through fountains, escalators, and parking lots with cars that are permanently in parking purgatory. Or Dragon Driftway, which is inspired by the sleek form of a Chinese dragon and uses that form to create a series of smooth, snake-like turns and a bumpy section of jumps. The Sonic and Sega and All-Stars in Racing and Transformed and Knuckles series themes their tracks well too. These tracks are little love letters to the classic Sega games that they're based on. The Monkey Ball courses are laid out like actual Monkey Ball mazes, the Night Stage is full of elaborate callbacks to that game's boss fights, but what's more interesting is how Sonic Transform adds in a little bit of a narrative element with scripted set pieces that change some of the courses. The Skies of Arcadia track starts with a normal driving section through a village, but on the final lap, the village is blown up and turns into a flying section. Without variety, identity, and depth, a track is just kind of forgettable. While modern track design is usually pretty strong, some earlier tracks in Mario Kart weren't very memorable. Due to technical limitations, the tracks in the Mode 7 Mario Karts couldn't be much more than flat tracks with different skyboxes. Some of Mario Kart 64's track design was hit or miss, but some of the tracks hinted at what Nintendo's approach to track design would evolve into. Bowser's Castle and DK's Jungle Parkway are intertwined with their theme, with unique sections that pair their track design with their unique settings. Bland track design might be the biggest shortcoming of another ambitious and very popular kart racer, Diddy Kong Racing. I hear people describe these tracks as just circles, and after revisiting them, I totally agree. Diddy Kong Racing has a total of 20 tracks, each tied to one of five generic themes, like winter, dinosaurs, the beach, medieval times, palette swaps? The tracks themselves don't feel ingrained into the themes. There isn't a real sense of identity in most of these tracks, so you could swap out the theme of one with another and it wouldn't feel out of place. Diddy Kong Racing did make up for its track design with its variety of vehicles, the cars, hovercrafts, and planes all control very differently. Tracks are playable with multiple vehicles, but most tracks in Diddy Kong Racing feel like they're really only designed with one vehicle in mind. While you can play with different vehicle types in multiplayer races, it's almost impossible to make them all feel unique without making one of the vehicles objectively better to use on any given track. The track design can't accommodate for multiple vehicles, so some end up being more fun to play than others. Diddy Kong Racing's multi-vehicle design lives on in Sonic Transformed and the modern Mario Karts. They each have sections dedicated to different vehicle types. Sonic Transformed has vehicles similar to Diddy Kong Racing with boats and aircraft. Mario Kart is more subtle with the vehicles, just changing the driving physics in the underwater and zero gravity segments and adding in some basic maneuvering in the gliding segments. They get the benefit of the variety that each new vehicle brings, but they don't have to deal with balancing each track over three different vehicle types.
