Maybe most importantly, the on-the-fly vehicle transformations give the track designers a ton of creative freedom to come up with new and interesting track designs. And that's great. Anything that helps create interesting tracks will also help keep players interested in the game. So we have tracks, but how do kart racers design their driving mechanics to keep all kinds of players happy? Where racing sims are more about using realistic driving techniques, kart racers simplify how their vehicles handle. You can drift around corners like it's nothing, fishtailing and spinouts are barely a problem. The cognitive load of just taking a kart around the track is way, way lower. But just because you don't have to think that hard about kart handling doesn't mean there isn't a technique to it. Kart racers make factors like racing lines and drifting less important, but more advanced players can still use them to get better times. And kart racers have added extra gameplay elements to reward skillful driving. Enter the mini turbo. Mini turbos are nearly universal in kart racers. Different games pick and choose from a lot of different flavors. Rocket starts, drafting, track surface features like zippers and ramps, but the most iconic might be the drift mini turbo. Drifting pulls double duty. It helps you smoothly take turns without losing much speed, but if you know what you're doing, you can also drift to build up turbos. In Mario Kart 64, Double Dash, and Mario Kart DS, these turbos would be built up by quickly turning back and forth while in the middle of a drift. More advanced players can drift all over the track and chain together a ton of these mini turbos. This is called snaking, and it became pretty controversial in Mario Kart DS. It created an extreme skill gap in online play. You either snaked around the track, or you lost. Nintendo recognized this skill gap and considered snaking to be an unintentional exploit. From Mario Kart Wii onwards, drifting mini turbos were charged up by just holding the drift. The change made the turbo easier to pull off, but it made it harder to chain drift turbos together without going off track, which closed the skill gap a bit. Mario Kart may have taken the inspiration for the change from another classic kart racer, Crash Team Racing. When you drift in Crash Team Racing, a red and green meter builds up. By hitting L1 while the meter is red, you will release a mini turbo. Crash Team Racing also lets you gain a boost by hopping off of the apex of ramps and bumps in the terrain. With these mechanics, chaining these drift turbos together with jumps separates the novices from the veterans, while still being easy to learn. Since the Wii, Mario Kart has adopted a very similar system with tricks. Sonic Transformed also uses Mario Kart's chargeable drifting with its own version of tricks. Here, you manually perform spins and flips while airborne, but if you hit the ground in the middle of a trick, you will crash and lose any boost that had already been built up. Drifts are important and fun to do, but maybe more important to advanced players are racing lines. The problem with racing lines is that they're pretty static, and they can sometimes make the optimal strategy a bit too predictable and dull. Kart racers have shaken up the racing line idea with speed-boosting collectibles. Mario Kart's coins, DKR's bananas, CTR's wumpa fruit. These collectibles add another strategic element that challenges players to make a choice, to either take a more optimal path or sacrifice the ideal racing line to build up your max speed for later. The combination of these different types of speed-boosting systems does wonders for the track design. The way a player thinks about the track layout becomes deeper than just the geometry of the turns. It makes players incorporate the behavior of their competitors into their decision-making, like whether or not the person in front of you has already grabbed your coins. It tweaks the optimal lines and makes you think about just which path is the right one. Many turbos and speed boosters give everyone from little kids to world champions plenty of chances to find something fun to do, and plenty of opportunities to improve the way they attack the track. Kart racers wouldn't be the same without item pickups. Bananas, shells, nitro crates, homing missiles, drones, stars, shields, coins, boosters. Items are the linchpin that lets novices play with experts without the game turning into a bloodbath. Skilled players may hate items, but items that mix luck and randomness are crucial in making the game palatable for newer players. And it's not like they turn the game into a Mario Party-esque factory of randomness. Skill still plays a big role, even if items do shake things up. Mario Kart, Crash Team Racing, and Sonic Transformed give items to players hitting an item box depending on what position they're in. Front runners get weaker defensive items like green shells and bananas, while players stuck in the back get huge, powerful weapons to try and catch up. Blue shells to target leaders, bullet bills to zoom ahead, red shells to zero in on players ahead of you, stars to become invincible and go off-road, and lightning to slow down everyone else all contribute to Mario Kart's comeback mechanics,

## Moonlighter and Recettear - Item Shop Games ~ Design Doc
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lko7osS0AE8

I love unexpected games, especially ones that mash up two genres into one complete package. The two combine into a beautiful idea that we couldn't have played otherwise. Over the past decade, one of my favorite mashups has been the item shop genre, a dungeon crawler crossed with a light store management sim. Two major games from two different studios have come out about just that, 2010's English translation of Recettear and 2018's Moonlighter. Recettear came out of absolutely nowhere to break new ground. Moonlighter is a dramatic refinement of the idea and puts its own spin on it. But the two games still have their flaws, both subtle and glaring. Let's take a look at them both and dissect how their mechanics mix together. Recettear came out of the hobbyist side of the Japanese indie game development scene. It's closer to a passion project than a full retail release with full retail expectations. It was definitely made on a budget, but Recettear makes up for that lack of polish with the novelty of its premise and wraps it in just enough charm to draw you in. Recettear is about a little girl who is stuck with the massive loans taken out by her deadbeat father. Deadbeat or dead, one of the two. Either way, she opens up a little RPG world item shop with the help of her father's loan shark fairy. Together, they run their new shop, Recettear, to pay off the loans. Your job is to keep up with the bills, or else the item shop will be repossessed and Recette will have to find a nice cardboard box to live in. You'll run the store day to day, haggle with the locals, and restock your supplies, either by buying from the marketplace or hiring the town's adventurers, following them into randomly generated dungeons, and ruthlessly selling that sweet, sweet loot. But not to little girls with chump change that don't buy anything and waste my time. Get out of my store! Recettear's premise works wonderfully as a game loop. It's really tough to run the shop without running to the dungeons to restock your shelves, and you can't dive into the dungeons too often or you won't make enough money in your shop to meet your weekly payment and keep the debt fairy away. The game is constantly flipping between the two distinct game styles, and it keeps the game fresher for longer than either part could do on its own. The dungeon crawler injects some action and it's fine for what it is, but the store management side is the game's biggest attraction. Store regulars show up to haggle with you or sell you new items, and you can figure out each customer's tendencies and needs. Your adventurer friends can even equip what they end up getting at your store, so you can cut them a sweet deal on the stuff they buy in order to make the dungeons easier. You can customize your shop to attract different clientele, which makes it feel like you're really putting your own spin on the store you're managing. The two styles are a smart, natural combo, and the game gets a bunch of points for being a novel mashup without feeling contrived. But it's not all cheery anime kids, labor law violations, and wacky hijinks. The game has a ton of heart, but its ultra-indie roots show up a little more often than you'd like. The story is presented in a visual novel style, with static backgrounds and sliding conversations. The localization work by Carpe Fulger is actually very good, so the story doesn't weigh down the rest of the experience. The soundtrack is fine, though it'll get a little repetitive before the end. Maybe a lot repetitive. Haggling with your customers in the shop is fun at first, but the process of haggling can become predictable after a while, and that takes away some of the charm. The dungeon crawling half is simplistic. The dungeon layouts aren't that complex, and it definitely feels like you're running through the same set of tunnels after a while. The visual style isn't very cohesive, with the 3D models clashing hard with the backgrounds and the 2D sprites. There's a bit of inventory management to think about, but nothing complicated. The combat is real basic. Attack animations have almost no weight and feel stiff. Your super moves aren't that interesting or tactically complex. It's really a bare minimum combat system, and it hasn't aged all that well, as there are tons of quality top-down dungeon crawlers that do this style of combat much better. None of these problems are deal-breakers, but they'll pile up as you play. Recettear is a game with a novel hook surrounded by just enough window dressing to make it playable. Good, even. It's fun, it's definitely interesting, and it's totally still worth playing, even today. But clearly there was an opportunity for another studio to take a second shot at the idea. The item shop genre sat in hibernation for years, with one or two attempts briefly flashing to life, but without a real high-effort release to duplicate or improve on what Recettear had done. Until this year. Until Moonlighter. In Moonlighter, you play as a shopkeeper's son who dreams of getting out from behind the counter and diving into the mysterious dungeons nearby to find treasure and glory. You tend the shop by day, and moonlight, eh? Eh? As an adventurer by night. Or by day if you want. Whatever. I'm not your boss. Go down and beat the monsters within to unlock the next dungeons to explore, and their true nature will slowly be revealed. It's super clear that Recettear is a major influence on the direction and structure of Moonlighter, but developer Digital Sun has clearly taken the concept and poured a lot of hard work into it. Moonlighter is a beautiful game. Excellent sprite work, silky animation, a pretty UI. It's got one of the best soundtracks of the year. The action controls well, hands down better than Recettear, with more interesting attack and movement options and meaningfully different weapon types to help you deal with a set of more complex enemies. The inventory management is fun. Some of the items have little curses on them that do things to themselves or other inventory items nearby. Some curses are bad, like the one that breaks the item if you take too much damage. Some are good, like sending a different item to your chest at home, which frees up space. The item curses and the way they play off of the other items in your inventory feels fresh and makes you think more tactically about what items you're bringing back from the depths. It reminds me a little of Resident Evil 4's attache case. From top to bottom, Moonlighter is polished in all the ways the very best indie games are polished. But under all the beauty and pomp is a strange problem. The game runs out of depth, way faster than usual. This is probably going to sound pretty harsh, maybe more than Moonlighter deserves, because it is fun, but the game's progression is so bizarre. Every time it introduces a mechanic that could act as a platform to add gameplay depth, it seems to get plastered over. It's not quite paper thin, but Moonlighter definitely feels like a beautiful facade was built around a set of underdeveloped mechanics. Moonlighter feels unfinished, but in exactly the opposite way to how many other games feel unfinished. Usually, unfinished indie games are missing the polish. That's definitely not the problem here. After about hour 4, there is basically nothing more the game teaches you, introduces, or lets you discover. Unlike Recettear, which keeps introducing new mechanics as you progress. The game's progression ramp just evaporates. The dungeons all feel the same, just rooms with different themed wallpaper and a few new enemies. The story never ever evolves. It's led by your mentor character who has nothing to say to you other than, Be careful in the dungeon! Think about your responsibilities! For literally the entire game. The rest of the characters don't pick up the slack either. The writing makes them more one note than the hearing test. That is, until the very end where the game throws a ridiculous plot twist out of nowhere. Nothing happens. Nothing happens. Nothing happens. Then something happens so hard that the story is sliced in half. But maybe the biggest disappointments are outside the dungeons, in the town and in the item shop mechanics. It's not that far off from Recettear on its surface, and Moonlighter does add a few interesting ideas to the mix. But the mechanics end up getting undercut and kill the budding strategic complexity that the game could and should have. In Moonlighter, you put items out on your shop tables and set their prices.
