The mechanics of golf work better with these numeric systems than the mechanics of most other sports. To appreciate how well it works for golf, let's see how it works in another sport. Let's say in a basketball RPG, when your character levels up, maybe your shot percentage would go up, or your steal percentage would go up. But it won't be as clear that you've actually improved. Making changes to probabilities like shot percentage doesn't necessarily feel like you're progressing, even when you are. Going from an 80% to an 85% chance to make a shot in basketball is a huge change, but in the moment to moment of the game, it will very rarely make a difference. The progress you've made means only 1 in 20 extra shots go in. You get the same problem in a lot of other sports. Football, baseball, soccer, the game has to, at some point, roll a random number or else a skilled player could figure out how to always hit home runs or sink every half court shot. They would look superhuman, and the sport wouldn't feel like the real sport anymore. That's not to say that it's impossible for an RPG to work in a different sport. Modes like the career modes in Madden, NHL, or the NBA 2K series are still plenty of fun, but feeling the progress you've made as a player is harder to detect, which makes the gameplay loop a little less rewarding and makes the RPG side of the game feel a little less satisfying. Even traditional RPGs outside of sports have to deal with this same problem when they use probability-based systems. Let's look at Fire Emblem. In the game, you get a preview of how likely your attacks will hit your opponent. In the earlier entries in the series, this number was completely accurate, i.e. a 95% chance to hit really did only miss 5% of the time, but the developers noticed a problem. The negative feeling of missing what felt like an almost sure hit stuck with players, and since the player's strategy can fall apart when they do miss, using real probabilities made the game a little less pleasant to play. So, the developers made a change for releases outside of Japan. The game will still say you have a 90 or a 95% chance to hit, but under the hood, the game will roll the dice twice and average the two values, making it much, much harder to get the numbers you need to actually miss a 95% attack. In Golf Story, as you level up and increase your stats, you can see your character improve just as clearly as you can see your damage numbers rise in a game like Final Fantasy. Your drive distance goes up, your slice and backspin instantly improve. Instead of getting trapped in a bunker, you can now hit the ball just far enough to clear it and land on the green. You feel like you've progressed your character every time you hit the ball, because your performance makes it clear that something has changed. It's that immediate feedback in the gameplay that makes progressing in the game feel more satisfying and makes golf RPGs in general so fun to play. Yeah, Golf Story has problems, there are too many fetch quests, the golfing is a little too easy, the game's narrative sometimes goes too long between tournaments and golf events, the tutorials are pretty sparse, it's glitchy, the humor is hit or miss sometimes, but Golf Story is still a solid game. Even with its faults, Golf Story wins you over with a lot of heart, and it's a welcome sight for a genre that is so neglected, but so promising.

## FFX VS FFXIII - Two Linear Games, Two Outcomes ~ Design Doc
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QMZMJDFe1kc

Final Fantasy XIII has a reputation it can't shake. When people talk about it, usually someone brings up that they think the game is too linear, especially in its environmental design. But just describing the game as linear doesn't tell the whole story. After all, Final Fantasy X has very linear maps as well, and people still love it. So what's the difference? Why is X so well liked, while XIII is one of the most divisive games in the series? Linearity is a big part of it, but the linearity of FFXIII bleeds into so much more than just the game's environmental design. So, let's take a look at X and XIII, and see how two linear games can be so different. We'll start with the story and worldbuilding. Both of these games have linear stories, without branching narrative paths. In FFX, the story is focused around Tidus, a young star athlete from the futuristic city of Zanarkand. After surviving a devastating attack on his home by a living, hurricane, whale, awful father, kaiju thing called Sin, Tidus is taken away to the post-post-apocalyptic land of Spira, where Sin has wreaked havoc for 1,000 years. Tidus soon joins a young summoner named Yuna, who sets out on a pilgrimage in order to obtain the power to defeat Sin. Final Fantasy X is super effective at getting players up to speed on the core story in the first 20 minutes. Here's Tidus. He plays underwater soccer in a huge city. He's kinda cocky. Implied daddy issues. Here's Sin. It attacks the big city. Primary villain established. Tidus gets taken to another world through Sin. Core premise is NOOOOO! After introducing you to the world and main story conflict, the game keeps filling in its setting at that same brisk pace. Every area you travel to explores an aspect of Spira, summoners, and Sin. In Besaid, you learn of the religion of Yevon, its summoners, and their role in defeating Sin. At Killika, Sin's power is demonstrated, the fiends that you fight in random battles are revealed to be malicious spirits of the dead, and you see first hand what summoners provide for the people of Spira. In Luka, you learn of the leadership in the Church of Yevon, the prejudice against the Albed, and even how the game's mini-game, Blitzball, brings together the people of Spira as one of the only sources of fun in a world of constant tragedy. Operation Miehen establishes why Sin cannot be fought through normal means. Even though you're locked into moving from one location to another, the game is structured to reveal the culture and history of Spira at an even pace, steadily building up the anticipation as your party gets closer and closer to their goal, the ruins of Zanarkand. Final Fantasy XIII is a bit more complex. It's set on the two warring worlds of Cocoon and Grand Pulse. The story is centered around a small group of people from Cocoon. After a complex series of events involving a small-scale rebellion against the militia of Cocoon, our group is cursed by a divine being known as a Pulse Falsi. This curse turns the group into Pulse Lasi. Pulse Lasi are the enemies of Cocoon. Enemies of Cocoon. Enemies of Cocoon. Enemy of Cocoon. Enemies of Cocoon. Enemies of the state. Enemy of the state. Pulse Falsi are Cocoon's enemies. They're the enemy. Lasi are super-powered agents of whichever Falsi chose them. All Lasi are given a Focus, a mission assigned to them by the Falsi through extremely vague visions. The party of newly branded Pulse Lasi must complete their Focus or be turned into mindless monsters called Seath. The group then sets out to find the truth of their Focus, evade the pursuit of Cocoon's militia, and do whatever they can to save both themselves and their home. The difference here is with the game's herky-jerky pacing. Key plot information in Final Fantasy XIII isn't as clear-cut as it is in Final Fantasy X, and the game just loves throwing tons of new information at you all at once. The game starts by jumping between three different perspectives, Lightning and Sazh, Snow, and Hope and Vanille, all in the middle of a pretty vague side conflict. What is Lightning after? Oh, she's after the Pulse Falsi. Here it is. Oh wait, no, that's not actually the Pulse Falsi, that's just the Vestige, which is like a building that holds the Falsi. What is a Pulse Falsi? No time for that, just look at the datalog. Now here's Snow and his child army. They're heroes, I guess? Here's the Psycomm soldiers. They're all from Cocoon, except Lightning, who is not a Psycomm soldier, she's a Guardian Corps soldier, which is different from Psycomm, I guess? Confused? Datalog. Where is this? Look at the skybox, this is all just vague sci-fi. FFXIII's story isn't really that complicated, but it's more convoluted and hard to follow than it needed to be. FFXIII leans on explaining fundamental aspects of its world through datalogs, rather than the actual events, which makes it tougher for newcomers to keep up with what's going on. The terms tend to be less straightforward to explain as well. Explaining things like Falsi, Lasi, and Seath, and the differences between Cocoon and Pulse Lasi, tend to be more demanding than explaining the terms in FFX, like Summoner, Sin, and Blitzball, and makes it just a bit harder to get into the flow of the game. Compared to X, XIII doesn't guide the player through this new world as clearly either. Outside of a few exposition dumps, most of the information about Cocoon and Pulse's culture is buried in datalogs. There isn't much in the way of recurring characters or even side plots either, as the story focuses on developing its six main characters. Yet the story still sometimes spins its wheels. Yes, Hope, I get that you want to murder Snow. He's gonna catch on if you keep death-staring at him. Can we please move on? In X, the people you meet along the pilgrimage give character to the world of Spira in a clear and digestible manner. The story in XIII makes more sense if you're already familiar with the world of Cocoon. The time that X spends building up its world alongside characters, XIII spends building up characters in a world that hasn't been fully built yet. All these little hang-ups make it harder to get into the flow of XIII's story, and since the game's linearity is done in service of progressing that story, these problems degrade the overall game experience. Now let's get into the environmental design for both games. Both have very linear maps. You know, just go from here to here. But there's more to it than that. Final Fantasy X does four key things that help distract from its own linearity. Pacing, level gimmicks, pit stops, and secret items. The pacing is quick. The areas in FFX are only about two or three screens long. You move on to the next locale before an area outstays its welcome. Many areas have unique gimmicks or mini-games. Dodging lightning, riding chocobos, blitzball, solving puzzles in the Cloister of Trials, or navigating a maze. Most areas have pit stops, small shops or other locations where you can learn about side plots and supporting characters. The old sage Machen tells you about the history of Spira. The rival summoner Donna gives the player another perspective on the responsibilities of the pilgrimage. The acolyte Shalinda represents the followers of Yevon. The shrewd merchant Awaka gives you special deals on items if you invest in them early. And the retired summoner Belgemine gives aeon combat challenges and tips. These little pit stops serve as a break in the core gameplay loop. The game still rewards exploration in each environment by sticking hidden chests and little secrets everywhere. You never know when you'll stumble into one of the many outbid primers or jack spheres. The game's fixed camera even plays into this, making it trickier and more rewarding to discover everything. All these subtle variations in side content serve to break up the monotony of X's environments. Most of FFXIII's environments are like the Mii and Hyrule in FFX, minus the NPCs, pit stops, and triple the length. Areas like the Fifth Ark in Chapter X just seem to go on and on and on. Move forward, fight. Move forward, fight. Cutscene. Move forward and fight. There are a couple gimmicks in Chapter IV and VI, but they're the exception, and they're pretty short anyway. Treasure chests are very rarely hidden. They're almost always placed at the end of a short branching path with an enemy guarding it. I know it's a cliche at this point, but these environments really are mostly just fancy hallways. There is one moment where XIII does take a small break from this formula. It happens in Chapter VII when you reach Hope's house and he reunites with his father. Every character gets to literally take a break and have some interesting conversations. It's a nice tonal shift, and the game really could have used more of them to break up the gameplay. You almost get another one at the start of Chapter VIII in the amusement park Nautilus, which is basically a stand-in for FFX's Golden Saucer. This perfect opportunity for mixing up the gameplay is completely wasted. The whole area is just another giant hallway that just happens to have a few NPCs that only talk to you as you pass them by. The area would have been much better with two or three simple mini-games, some special shops, maybe play around with these chocobos, or

## Designing Narrative Choice - Add Branching Paths to Game Stories Without a AAA Budget ~ Design Doc
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gdt5zCdXoSc

Big budget games are getting harder to make.
Cutting-edge AAA games get more expansive, more fluidly animated, and more beautiful every year.
That means more assets need to be made, more detail needs to go into each piece, more polish needs to be applied.
All of this needs to be done by the professional artists, animators, riggers, musicians, and programmers of the gaming industry, and they don't work for free.
But even with the astronomical budgets of modern AAA games, there's an ironic twist.
There are game design problems that get harder and harder to solve as a game scales up.
The more work that goes into making a game, the harder it is to infuse it with meaningful narrative choice.
The ability to play with narrative choice is one of the great strengths of video games as an art medium, but narrative choice needs to be thought through carefully, and all paths of that choice need to be developed.
Otherwise, if you're not careful, if a game designer or script writer could put narrative choice in wherever they think it's most interesting, the production process of a game can get out of hand very quickly.
So what are some ways that game developers add meaningful narrative choice efficiently?
Let's say we're making an RPG that follows the plot of Star Wars Episode IV.
Early on, you want to let the player make a really interesting narrative choice for Luke.
He could follow Ben, become a Jedi, and save the galaxy.
Or he could stay as a moisture farmer on Tatooine.
If you leave with Ben, your game should probably develop into a pretty standard RPG.
Action sequences, dialogue options, pretty similar to Knights of the Old Republic.
But if you stay, it wouldn't really make sense to have a bunch of fight scenes.
Instead, the Luke as moisture farmer game might feel a bit more like a Star Wars themed Harvest Moon.
A completely different experience.
The setting would be unique, game mechanics would be completely different, the music would change, entirely different creatures and people would have to be modeled.
If you had a big set piece action sequence on the galaxy saving branch, you'd probably want to create something equally impressive on the other side, or else the branches would feel out of balance.
You'd need way more people and way more time to build up both choices.
By giving the player just this one narrative choice, the studio would need to create two essentially unique games and bundle them into one disc.
But this example is a bit overboard.
If it were that hard to add narrative choice, we wouldn't have many games with it at all.
So, how do game designers add what feels like meaningful narrative choice to their games without creating an avalanche of work?
Well, for one, you can make the choices not last nearly as long.
If you can make a choice, but resolve that choice before too long, you can rejoin the central plot thread.
For example, Night in the Woods lets you pick which friend to hang out with on several nights.
Hanging out lets you get more insight on each of the characters, but the next morning will play out the same way no matter what choice you make.
The choices are isolated, and this can encourage multiple playthroughs, but using this technique can cause other problems too.
Shadow the Hedgehog has a bunch of splitting paths that unlock as you make choices during the earlier stages, letting you sort of plinko your way through to the end of the game.
It even diagrams all the paths that you've taken, so you can see exactly where you are.
Unfortunately, once you've played through the game a few times, you have to slog through big chunks of the story that you've already played to get to any new content.
Also, Shadow the Hedgehog is terrible, and it's really hard to make a bad game good by having a lot of different endings.
Speaking of that, another way to get the feeling of choice in the game without blowing your budget is by having multiple endings.
If the ending hinges on one choice, especially near the end, you don't have to make as much content for each path.
And you also avoid that replay fatigue problem if you let the player save right before they make that choice.
You can also make a lot of small choices add up, instead of having a single major choice decide your ending.
A lot of Bioware games took this route, with a light and dark meter in Knights of the Old Republic and the Paragon Renegade system in Mass Effect.
Throughout the game, you accrue points that determine character alignment.
Meet certain thresholds throughout the story, and new options open up to you, including distinct endings.
Fable and Infamous did something similar too.
Dishonored has a more modern take on this.
There's an order and chaos meter that you affect throughout the game.
The world changes as you move towards either extreme, which helps make the world feel impacted by small choices that you've made.
However, these meter systems often have a problem.
It's very easy to make the middle path uninteresting.
If you don't act like the saintliest saint or the most devilish devil, your in-game options are limited.
A lot of the most interesting powers are locked away at the extremes, and a lot of the more interesting story options are too.
The middle path can result in underpowered characters, no faction to really call your own, and NPCs that criticize you for the choices you've made anyway.
This makes players want to pick a side and stick with it always, which ironically makes a game full of choices feel a lot more linear.
Telltale Adventure games have lots of small decision points too, but they often run into a different problem.
If you make a choice between option A or option B, and both have to make sense in the rest of the plot, the game shouldn't just hand-wave away the implications of one of the paths.
Take Telltale's Game of Thrones.
In it, you have to pick one of your advisors to become your right-hand man.
Spoiler alert! The other one betrays you!
For one of the advisors, the reasons for their betrayal make sense.
But if you choose to promote them instead, the other side completely breaks character to betray you.
Just because both of these possibilities needed to rejoin the plot at the same point.
Another strategy that adds choice while keeping production costs down is to reuse as much of the game as possible, but give new context depending on the path you're taking.
Tactics Ogre does an amazing job here.
The game takes place on a small number of discrete maps which you travel through and fight on throughout the story.
There are a few points in the main plot where you will pick a side to ally with, which completely changes which NPCs you encounter, fight for, and against.
But the maps all remain the same.
You might be fighting north to south for one faction, marching towards a southern port town, while if you took the other path, you'd be fighting on the same map marching south to north, looking to besiege a northern castle.
You get a completely different story and really feel like you've made a major choice without a ton of extra work for the developers.
Like Tactics Ogre, Chrono Cross also reuses large parts of the game, but adds a lot of narrative choice through the interactions you have with your party members.
The game lets you recruit literally dozens of unique characters, but many of them are blocked off in side quests or story options.
Make a choice to save a character, and not only can they join your party, but entirely unrelated branches of the story will unlock later on, each in turn having their own characters to recruit.
Make a different choice, and the game unfolds completely differently.
The characters you recruit will all say the same lines in a given cutscene, but they'll say them according to their own verbal tics and mannerisms.
Different events will happen in the same map location depending on which characters you've recruited before.
Chrono Cross does have paper-thin characterization for most of the extended cast, especially once they join your party, but the game gives you so many options, and the same story advances in so many different ways depending on the path you take, that your choices do feel impactful.
Lots of these techniques work best in relatively large games, but how do smaller indie studios with tiny staffs and shoestring budgets make games with interesting choice?
Actually, that irony I talked about earlier works in their favor.
The production value expectations that get baked into AAA game development make it more time-consuming to create the branching paths that come with meaningful choice.
But, if you don't have to make something as pretty as a AAA game, a lot of that problem goes away.
Less graphical fidelity for each asset makes it easier for a small team to make more of them.
It's much faster to make branching storylines for a game that looks like Final Fantasy Tactics than for a game that looks like Final Fantasy XV.
Better development tools over the last 10 years have also made it easier to do more work in less time.
Narrative choice is a tricky problem in game development.
If you let it, it can explode the scope of a project and slow down production on even the highest budget games.
Finding the right combination of meaningful choice and handling how that choice plays out over the course of a game can mean the difference between an immersive and personally meaningful experience and vaporware.

## The Forgotten Depth of Kingdom Hearts ~ Design Doc
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zcYSbfrO5uo

Square Enix is toiling away in their gold mine, working on their next big JRPG. It's a big project, maybe the most anticipated game in their storied history. It'll be a milestone, for their fans, and likely for the future of the company. Kingdom Hearts 3. Square Enix just announced that the game will be ready sometime in the next three years. Now, if I just put three years into my custom-made Square Release Schedule Translator, count for production values and delays, it spits out a release date of... never. While we wait for never to get here, we'll look at a rather understated and often forgotten aspect of the original Kingdom Hearts' combat, the Tech Point system. Kingdom Hearts is known for its reliable production schedule, sensible naming conventions, and flawless writing. That was undeniable proof that we totally owned you, lamers. Listen to those cheers, man! You don't get to decide if you're a hero or not. They do. And they've already made up their minds. Xion! Who else will I have ice cream with? This is my favorite series, and after all of these years, the first game is still hands down my personal favorite. And its combat system holds up extremely well. While the later games got more flashy and combo heavy, I prefer the slower, weighty, and more challenging combat of the first game. While Kingdom Hearts 1 was not perfect, and it could be kinda clunky at times, I felt that it had the least amount of fluff in its combat design. As most of your combat options and abilities had a clear purpose with dodge rolls, magic, guarding, special attacks, and other various skills. Kingdom Hearts 2 had a bit of a dominant strategy problem, where unless you were playing on the critical difficulty, your best option in combat more often than not turned out to be just wailing on enemies with your basic attacks. Kingdom Hearts 1 and Kingdom Hearts 2 are button mashers. The first game certainly has its fair share of mindlessly hacking through enemies, but there was still a bit of depth. Compared to its sequel, Kingdom Hearts 1 has a bit more emphasis on timing and defensive maneuvers, and the individual moment-to-moment gameplay felt more engaging, partially thanks to a feature I wish more single-player games would adopt, its bonus experience point system, tech points. Tech points were a mechanic exclusive to Kingdom Hearts 1 that granted bonus experience points for taking special actions in combat, like hitting weaknesses, using ice on fire enemies or vice versa, parrying attacks by striking at just the right moment, guarding attacks, or deflecting projectiles back at enemies all give the player tech points. What makes this mechanic awesome is that it rewards players for exploiting your opponent. You don't only level up from taking enemies out, you gain EXP faster from fighting properly, and basically getting good. This mechanic makes sure that the little nuances in the combat system don't get lost in the shuffle and helps make the different enemy types feel more unique. The game teaches you about the system very early on. Parrying and tech points are taught in the optional fights against the kids on Destiny Islands. When you parry against Selfie's Whip, not only does it block her attack, it bounces off and hits her right on the forehead, giving you an additional 2 EXP, double what you normally get by just winning the fight. Another example, when you hit Wakka with his own projectiles, it stuns him, causing him to lob his next couple shots. The fights with all of the kids become much easier and more rewarding once the player gets the hang of parrying. It's not only a great way to level up quickly at the start, but also a good survival tactic. Most of the game's enemies and bosses have some attack that can either be parried, guarded, or exploited for tech points. The game also plays around with this system with special enemies like the White Mushrooms that play a kind of magic Simon Says game for tech points and other various items. The idea of a full progression system directly tied to player skill is great and subtly different than what most other RPGs have. A lot of other games have bonus XP systems, but the systems often work in really arbitrary ways. Some implement it as a random bonus, like in Persona 3's roulette system. Sometimes it's a passive bonus like the Moon Confidant in Persona 5, or an item like the EXP share in Pokemon. Final Fantasy X hands out bonus experience for getting overkills, but a player can get around the system by using a ton of MP, or just by fighting wimpy enemies. So it doesn't really incentivize you to get a deeper understanding of your opponents. A ton of RPGs implement a vague end-of-battle report that grades and rewards you based on your general performance, but it does very little to actually guide you into playing better. I just destroyed these guys, what do you mean I got three stars? Why do I keep getting negative grade? What does finesse mean? There are some games that take a similar approach to Kingdom Hearts in using XP as an incentive for mastery and taking risks. Bravely Default rewards extra experience based on how fast you win the fight. The World Ends With You has an interesting risk versus reward system that gives you more points for voluntarily taking on more fights in a row. Ys Origins gives more XP for keeping a high combo count. Batman Arkham Asylum, even though it's not an RPG, rewards both high combo counts as well as varying your combat strategy. The key aspect in these games, and in Kingdom Hearts, is that bonus XP is an active reward that directly encourages you to get better at the combat, rather than granting you experience for brute force, random luck, or just reaching some arbitrary point in the game. Though sometimes those all happen in Kingdom Hearts as well. Positive reinforcement and feedback play an important role in teaching game mechanics to players. Kingdom Hearts is a game where the mastery of its mechanics lead immediately to in-game rewards, so becoming a better player in Kingdom Hearts turns into a faster progression. This idea of tying skill to progression in a single-player experience is seen in more modern games too. The difficulty of Dark Souls is an offshoot of this idea. It turned the process of mastering combat from a recommendation to a requirement to progress at all. It's very unlikely for a player in Dark Souls to just hack their way through the game, and it's a better game for it. Kingdom Hearts' bonus XP system turned what could have been just another action RPG button masher into a game with a surprising amount of depth and makes Kingdom Hearts a game that was just a bit ahead of its time. Kingdom Hearts 2

## Good Design, Bad Design - The Best & Worst of Graphic Design in Games ~ Design Doc
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bE_ZuNp1CTI

So, last month, Persona 5 pretty much consumed my life. And if I had just one takeaway, it would be that it has the slickest UI I've ever seen. My god! It's so dynamic! So smooth! So stylish! It's gorgeous! The character is just running through the victory screen! That is so cool! Sorry. So, in honor of Persona 5, I just want to talk about some graphic design. To put it broadly, graphic design is visual communication. Applied to games, it's your menus, UI, camera work, color choice, font choice, animation, character design, your presentation of information. There's a lot of overlap between graphic design and art, but graphic design is about more than aesthetics. Good graphic design in a game is like a good translator, where it seamlessly and stylishly communicates to its players and makes immersing yourself in a game a little bit easier. Bad graphic design is like a bad translation, an obstacle, making it more of a chore to get into and taking some of the shine off a game. I'm going to highlight some great and, well, terrible graphic design in games. But before we dive in, here are some rules. These examples are chosen based on a combination of style and practicality in their design. These aren't ranked, since trying to decide what is the best graphic design is, well, impossible. Unless it's Persona 5. If there is an example that you are fond of that doesn't make it here, post it in the comments. I'll probably do another one of these, so it may show up there. Anyway, first up, a masterclass in communicating game mechanics through visuals. Good design. One of the biggest challenges in many stealth games is a lack of clarity. Too often, whether you can be seen or heard by an enemy is a mystery. It can lead to some frustrating trial and error gameplay. A good stealth game is like a good puzzle game. They work best when you can see all the pieces in front of you, just waiting to be solved. Mark of the Ninja is a game with some very intuitive UI and visual cues to tell the player everything they need to know so they can confidently plan out their moves. In Mark of the Ninja, visibility is treated as a binary system. You are either hidden in shadow or exposed in light. Characters and objects in shadow are nicely defined by white outlines and are fully colored when they're in the light. Even your own visibility is smartly indicated by subtle changes in lighting and blurring effects. Any area blocked by a wall is darker until it's within the player's point of view. Any rooms that you are adjacent to are blurred and clear up as you peek through vents and doors. Sound in Mark of the Ninja is just as clear-cut. As you make noise, the range of each sound is represented by a ring. The ring's size is dependent on the sound itself. Running will produce medium-sized rings and louder actions like breaking objects will make larger rings. Every one of your tools is laid out in your HUD. They are also conveyed through icons on objects in the environment like bells or pots. These help make your tools easy to use, which lets you focus on solving the puzzle rather than being caught up in the game's mechanics. It may not make the game more immersive or even that much more stylish, but Mark of the Ninja's UI is super practical and makes playing the game feel like second nature. Bad design. Now, bad graphic design doesn't make a bad game. Smash 4 is great, but the menus... eh, not so much. Smash 4's main menu represents the thin line between success and failure in graphic design. On first glance, it looks fine, like a more colorful version of the menus from Super Smash Bros. Brawl. But as you start clicking around, you'll notice a problem. The organization of the menu is strange, which makes navigating the menus feel clunky. The menu elements have an inconsistent look, and aside from the giant smash button, there's a serious lack of visual hierarchy. The objects in the menu aren't arranged by their importance. The multiplayer is the most prominent option here, as it should be, but the other options are all fighting for your attention. The biggest offender in Smash 4's menu is right here. Games and more. That's the vaguest title ever. That's like naming the button, here's some more stuff, I don't know. Now Brawl and Melee had their priorities straight. You had single player, versus, online, vault, options, and data. There you go. The essential categories are nice and organized. But in Smash 4, single player, vault, and options are all shoved into games and more. Other menu items are thrown around at random. Why is Trophy Rush, a single player minigame, not in the stadium option with the other minigames? Why is challenges not placed in vault or single player? Why do custom moves have to be set in a separate menu, and not just on the character select screen? Why is Smash Tour anywhere? Smash 4's UI issues don't stop there. The UI in Smash Tour is chaotic and overly flashy, to the point that makes the game harder to play. Smash 4's sloppy design is especially strange. The designer worked on Kirby's Air Ride and the last two Smash Bros. games, none of which have these problems. But with the way the menu is now, it makes finding stuff a total pain until you just memorize it. Good design. Brutal Legend is a game I desperately want to love, but I only like. It's one of those games that seems to be going one way, but then it becomes something else entirely, and it's just kind of... eh. Despite that, Brutal Legend has three really cool things going for it. One, the main character is just Jack Black being himself, and that's usually a good time. Decapitation! Two, exploring the open world and seeing Double Fine's vision of a crazy heavy metal fantasy world is amazing. And three, the UI absolutely nails its theme. Designed by Joe Kowalski, Brutal Legend's graphic design proudly wears its inspirations on its sleeve. The type, especially on the headers, is very similar to the bold, angular, and gothic typefaces of logos from iconic metal bands like Iron Maiden, Def Leppard, Motorhead, and Black Sabbath. The in-game encyclopedia is presented in a high schooler's notebook, the start of every mission is the cover art of a worn-out album, every UI element, tutorial, and even certain cutscenes use a distinct illustration style inspired by medieval and Norse woodcuts, which mesh extremely well with the heavy metal fantasy. The interface also has high contrast with the black and white standing out nicely from the colorful landscapes. I love Brutal Legend's UI in general, but the real standout here is the main menu. You sure you're ready for this? Because what I hold in my hand is not just going to blow your mind, it's going to blow your soul. The main menu is an interactive FMV that goes through a custom-made gatefold album of the game itself. Every option is on a different part of the album. New Game and Continue are in the inside cover, Chapter Select is found in the back where you'd find the tracklist, Multiplayer is in the record sleeve, and Options and Extras are the record's A and B sides respectively. This menu oozes creativity, and it also makes a few smart decisions to keep the theme from getting in the way of this menu's usability. In the raw footage, the type isn't actually on the album itself. It was edited in post to allow it to be made in different languages, and the footage is sped up to keep navigation from feeling too sluggish. There's a great behind-the-scenes video, which I'll link below, that shows the designer working on the UI of the game. It goes over some of the design and editing challenges, like matching different takes, or adding out little mistakes. It's great if you're interested in video editing. Overall, Brutal Legend's menu is one of the more creative uses of FMV that I've ever seen in a game. Bad design. Let's just get right to it. Mario Party 8 is a total eyesore in its menu and UI design. It's functional, barely, but this presentation is just really poor. Here's a weird thing. The main menu is at a 16 by 9 aspect ratio, but the game itself is shown at a 4 by 3 ratio. It's jarring and unnecessary. The typography here is some of the worst I've ever seen. The type in the main menu items are off-center. The kerning, the spacing between individual letters, is uneven in spots. But the biggest issue here is the dump truck of different typographic styles in the menus. Most designers would recommend keeping your different font choices and styles down to about two or three at a time. The main menu alone has up to five different fonts and type treatments. Here, here, here, here, and here. This isn't even the worst example of this in this game. Mario Party 8's typography inconsistently switches between using multiple outlines, drop shadows, and gradients for contrast. Like fonts, it's a good idea to use these effects sparingly on text. But instead, the game likes to use all three of these effects at once. Look at the text that appears at the start of someone's turn. The font here has two outlines, one of which has an ugly golden gradient, and there's also a drop shadow in between this line and the red fill. This is a typographic nightmare. There's no cohesiveness between modes either. The menus, board game screen, mini game screen, and the results screen all have something unique and terrible in their type. It's just all over the place. Good design. I can't say I'm really into the Dead Space series because I'm what some might call a big man baby coward, but Dead Space has some nice UI. It's almost like a direct evolution of Metroid Prime's helmet HUD, where

## Nintendo Switch - The History in the System ~ Design Doc
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bNr0aD1YbHA

The Nintendo Switch is finally here. It's a hybrid of console and portable systems, forged by the lessons learned over 30 years of hardware development and steeped in the DNA of a company that loves to do things their own way. For Nintendo, each new piece of hardware is a chance to make a fresh start, but nothing is completely new. If you look closely, you can see patterns, ideas echoing through time. Some ideas changed the industry, some completely flopped, and some ideas just weren't quite ready yet. But they all reveal bits and pieces of the identity of the company that created them. To understand what's in store for the Switch's future, maybe we can look for answers in Nintendo's past. Every Nintendo system comes with a piece of iconic hardware, its controller. The Switch and its Joy-Con controllers are no different. Out of the box, you'll be able to choose from several different control schemes depending on the game you're playing. Having so many different controller options has been common for Nintendo, going back to the very beginning. The NES first came bundled with its original rectangular controllers. Soon after, Nintendo released the NES Advantage, which had an arcade stick, turbo controls, and could plug into both Player 1 and Player 2 ports at the same time. Then came the NES Max, which had this awful, terrible, circle pad-looking thing instead of just a regular D-pad. Even in the mid-90s, very late in the console's life cycle, Nintendo released the NES Controller 2, a dog bone-shaped redesign of the original rectangle. The SNES controller was more comfortable to hold and added more buttons to allow for more complex games, but the design stayed the same throughout the SNES era. On the N64, Nintendo started supporting more than one control scheme on a single controller. You could grip the three-pronged controller in two different ways. It was... unique, and sometimes painful. But even though game designers were given more options, just about every game was designed for the controller to be held with one hand on the analog stick. Starting in the early 2000s on the Game Boy Color and Game Boy Advance, Nintendo started experimenting with motion controls. Kirby's Tilt and Tumble, Yoshi's Topsy-Turvy, and WarioWare Twisted came with custom hardware embedded in the game cartridges to detect tilting and shaking. The DS didn't support motion controls, but still had plenty of new features. It added more buttons for more complex handheld games, a built-in microphone, and its biggest innovation was its touch-capable second screen. Smartphones weren't nearly as widespread at the time the DS was released, so the DS was one of the few places where games with touch controls were being developed. Having two closed screens was used to great effect on the DS and later the 3DS, but the idea did not translate as well when Nintendo tried to adapt dual-screen gaming to the Wii U. The love affair with motion controls kicked into high gear with the Wii, but the results were mixed. Wii Sports, arguably still the best game ever built for motion controls, was available at the launch for the Wii, but more games of that quality were few and far between. The Wii Motion Plus was able to improve the responsiveness of the hardware, but it wasn't cheap, and it only made a difference in a few games. For every game that used motion controls well, like Wii Sports and WarioWare Smooth Moves, you can find dozens of others that just shoved it in as an afterthought. Twilight Princess had a ton of waggle, Wii Music was a disaster through and through, and look at all this shovelware! The basic Wii Remote was designed primarily around motion controls, but Nintendo knew that there would still be games released on the Wii that would work best with a standard controller. Classic games available on the Virtual Console, for instance, weren't designed to use motion controls at all, so Nintendo made more controllers, like in the NES days. The Wii Classic Controller had a design that echoed the SNES controller, which worked great for those older games, but also had a more modern layout, with analog sticks and four shoulder buttons, which made it perfect for more complex games. Nintendo also released the Wii Classic Controller Pro, which felt even nicer to hold. After the Wii, Nintendo was again wrestling with how to support traditional games while still trying to make their next console innovative. The novelty of motion control games was wearing off, so Nintendo needed a new hook. This is the new controller for Wii U. With the Wii U GamePad, Nintendo added a big screen in the middle of a traditional controller to allow new game styles without hindering traditional designs too much. But because of hardware limitations and the expense of each GamePad, Nintendo only allowed one to be connected to a single console at a time. Nintendo seemed unsure of the Wii U's main hook, and to try to fix this problem, they threw the kitchen sink at it. In one way or another, the Wii U works with half of all controllers Nintendo has ever released. The Wii U GamePad, a new Wii U Pro Controller, everything ever released on the Wii, a straight-up 3DS, and you can even hook up an adapter for GameCube controllers. Granted, only for one game, but eh. The flood of controllers led to practical problems. Super Smash Bros. for the Wii U let you choose between all of these options, which led to an explosion of control schemes. With so many options, it makes it tough for a game designer to focus on making each control option feel good. But the biggest problem with the Wii U GamePad was with its main gimmick, the center screen. It was rarely used effectively. Star Fox Zero used it, but it felt clunky, overwhelming, and a bit forced. Some games that could have used the screen to do amazing things that wouldn't be possible on a traditional controller were never even developed. I'm looking at you, Pokemon Snap 2. It's never gonna happen. What we've talked about so far is a history of standard controllers. But for every generation, Nintendo also put out weird hardware tailor-made for specific games. The NES had the Zapper and the Power Pad, the SNES had the Super Scope for a small handful of shooters, and the mouse which worked for Mario Paint and a few strategy games. Then came the bongos, the Hey You Pikachu microphone thing, the Mario Party microphone thing, the Wii microphone thing, the balance board, all the plastic crap you could stick a Wii Remote into, and even the cancelled Vitality Sensors showed that Nintendo always tries to work unusual control schemes into their systems, even if those were abandoned almost immediately. The repeating pattern you see through Nintendo's history is a broadening of possibilities with control schemes. The Switch does this by just including everything. Every control scheme that Nintendo has released before is showing up on the Switch. Motion controls, a touchscreen, a complete set of buttons, and Bluetooth support for connecting whatever random controller idea they'll have in the future. This, hopefully, is a refined version of what the Wii U was trying to accomplish. But all of the pitfalls of having too many control options apply here too. There could also be a problem with how the Switch supports touch gaming. When the Switch is docked, players won't have a touchscreen handy, so game designers have to consider that limitation. There are even a few games that won't be playable on your TV at all, but even if it's tough to work around, it's not an impossible problem to solve. We've already seen games adapt touch controls to standard controllers successfully. Console and PC ports of mobile games do this all the time. The Switch gives developers the opportunity to build or port games with just about any modern game design. What remains to be seen is whether developers take the time and effort to make something that feels right for their game. So, the Switch's controller looks solid, but Nintendo changes more than just the controller between generations. For instance, Nintendo loves Rumble. They created the Rumble Pak, which put force feedback in a home console for the first time. It was such a big hit, Nintendo shoved it into the Game Boy Color as fast as they could, even though the system wasn't at all designed to let you plug in peripherals. Instead, Nintendo stuck a motor inside the Game Boy cartridge itself. Put a AAA battery into Pokemon Pinball, Top Gear Pocket, or, uh, Disney's The Little Mermaid 2 Pinball Frenzy, and you get Rumble on the go. All of Nintendo's consoles going forward, the GameCube, the Wii, and the Wii U, were designed with Rumble built in from the beginning. The Switch is shipping with HD Rumble, which promises much better fidelity. One-Two-Switch uses HD Rumble to mimic the feeling of marbles rolling around in a box, and first reports are that the tech is really impressive. But cool tech doesn't guarantee there will be games that put it to good use. We might have to wait for a new WarioWare game to explore what HD Rumble can really do. Each Joy-Con comes with HD Rumble, but the right Joy-Con has one special feature, an IR sensor. IR tech has been used in older Nintendo products to do a bunch of different things. The Game Boy Color tried to replace the physical link cable and let two systems communicate with an IR sensor at the top. But it was unreliable and finicky to use. Hardly any games supported it. The sensor would only work if your systems were this close to each other, and you never touched the Game Boy while it was trying to transmit data. You couldn't even trade Pokemon with this thing, which is probably for the best. I mean, losing a shiny Charizard in a trade because someone bumped your Game Boy would have broken a lot of hearts. Nintendo abandoned IR tech for wireless communication, but brought it back on the Wii and the Wii U. IR works great for sensing depth, and some of the minigames in 1-2-Switch use it for

## Paper Mario: Color Splash's Combat ~ Design Doc
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=39l8AEa6rY8

Paper Mario Color Splash is... okay? I mean, it's pretty to look at and the exploration is pretty good, but man, that combat is real bad. It's a step down from what Paper Mario's developer, Intelligent Systems, has created before. Regardless of where you stand on Color Splash, the most common criticism has been the very flawed battle system. This comes from how Nintendo and Intelligent Systems have tried to step away from the series' RPG roots, while still holding on to core systems that fall apart without those roots in place. In a nutshell, Color Splash and its predecessor, Sticker Star, use a light turn-based combat system where attacks are done with disposable items. It's a departure from the more traditional turn-based combat of the original Paper Mario and its GameCube sequel, The Thousand Year Door. But the two styles have some similarities. Let's call the two styles Classic Paper Mario for the two older games, and Modern Paper Mario for the two newer ones. The fundamentals of Modern Paper Mario are not that different from Classic Paper Mario, but the quality suffers from the simplifications. The combat of Color Splash and Sticker Star lack in four key areas. Engagement, depth, customization, and incentive. Let's start with engagement. A good combat system gets players engaged, something that Color Splash fails to do for two reasons, action commands and health. Action commands are a defining aspect of Mario RPGs. For every attack that the player uses or defends against, a little bun prompt or mini-game appears. Succeed and attacks become more powerful or your defense improves. Classic Paper Mario used action commands perfectly. They were varied and just short enough to keep battles active without being too tedious. In Classic Paper Mario, action commands had variety. You might pull the stick back, hold buttons, draw, shoot targets, and more. But in Modern Paper Mario, it's just time presses, time presses, time presses, mash, and more time presses. It's a big reason why combat is so damn tedious in Color Splash. Even the UI in Color Splash is a downgrade. It takes five to six inputs for an action that should only take two. When all attacks are performed the same way, it makes battles blend together, and your engagement in any one battle will drop. It's not just action commands that make battles more tedious. Changes in how the health system is handled make for a worse experience as well. One thing I love about Classic Paper Mario was the use of low damage numbers in combat. Unlike more traditional RPGs like Final Fantasy or Persona, which use huge arbitrary numbers for damage, every individual point of damage matters, and you get a better sense of how powerful you and your opponent really are. Seeing an 8 show up for a big attack when smaller ones show a 2 or 3 gives some real weight to those big attacks. The way Classic Paper Mario used low damage numbers made fights more engaging, as it let the player do the mental math to figure out the most efficient way to win. Combine the small damage numbers with an armor system that subtracts damage from each hit, and all of a sudden attacks feel very different from each other. For example, multi-hit moves like Bow's Smack might have higher damage output, but they are weak against enemies with high defenses, where moves with big single strikes are more effective. A simpler battle system lets the player think more deeply about what is actually happening in combat. None of these systems apply to Color Splash. Enemies don't have health bars, and your attacks don't display damage numbers. Enemy damage is only indicated by their color draining. It's a fun idea, and a cool visual motif, but it doesn't actually give the player a good sense of how strong their attacks really are. It's all for nothing anyway, because most enemies will go down in a single attack. I mean, for goodness sake, a normal Shy Guy goes down on the first strike of your weakest jump, which then will stomp him five extra times just to rub it in. I honestly can't tell if there's a difference in damage between the normal jump and the hop slipper. I mean, the enemy is still super dead. I just had to press the button a bit more. Color Splash took out information and made its action commands tedious, which makes the game's combat feel mindless. And because of that, one of the strong suits in classic Paper Mario becomes a chore, something to just get out of the way instead of something fun. Color Splash and Sticker Star's combat don't fail because they're too easy. They fail because there is so little to consider. Classic Paper Mario games aren't exactly challenging, but they aren't really pushovers, and they definitely aren't mindless. They gave you a ton of different options in combat, from normal attacks, special moves, items, star powers, and partners. Your options were complemented with plenty of enemy types, plus your limited pool of FP made you mix up your tactics. Part of the fun in combat was finding the most efficient strategies. Your options in Sticker Star and Color Splash mostly come down to either jump, hammer, heal, or thing. Yeah, thing. Just like classic Paper Mario, you do have to pay some attention to how enemies are set up, but it doesn't really mean much. There's practically no strategy to combat because four out of five times, you can win the fight in your first turn. There just isn't enough time spent for a complex strategy to play out, and the simple strategy works just as well anyway. If the fight just happens to be too hard, try using one of your zillion thing cards that will literally win the fight for you. Most of your overpowered attacks don't really have any real limitations, unless you count the pain system. Similar to mana or magic points, classic Paper Mario limited the player's power with FP, or flower points, which is there to prevent you from spamming your most powerful abilities. Intelligent Systems made an effort to strip out RPG elements in Sticker Star by getting rid of FP entirely, and instead made attacks inventory-based. This was often cited as one of the most frustrating aspects of the game. Color Splash would try to make the system less frustrating by making items more plentiful, and try to balance it with a pseudo-FP system in the form of the paint meter. In order for your cards to do any significant damage, they have to be painted, which depletes the paint meter. The problem is the amount of paint you use is so tiny and you are constantly tripping over paint refills, which makes the system borderline pointless. Granted, there are the fire and ice flower cards that do take up a significant amount of paint, but you have plenty of other more powerful options than those two, and you can get the fire and ice flower cards pre-painted anyway. If instead, the game raised the cost of paint across the board and made pre-painted cards more rare, that would make your attacks more significant, add strategy to combat, and it would make the upgrades to your paint capacity actually mean something. Speaking of upgrades, a huge sticking point in Sticker Star was how there wasn't much incentive for the player to fight random enemies. In Color Splash, their rewards for battles are cards, coins to buy even more cards, paint to refill your meter, and scrap hammers which upgrade your already huge paint capacity. Coins could have been a worthwhile reward if the game's economy wasn't absolutely busted. Coins are found everywhere and you can easily reach the coin cap in just a few hours. Despite having a pseudo-EXP system with the hammer scraps and paint meter, there is still no strong incentive to fight. After about one or two upgrades, the additional paint doesn't really feel needed, nor does it really open up any new possibilities in combat. The only reason I fought random enemies was that it was faster to just fight them than it was to try running away. In the end, every battle incentive boils down to just getting more cards, but with Color Splash's battle system as basic as it is, that really isn't much of an incentive at all. We still haven't talked about the most frustrating aspect of modern Paper Mario's combat, the lack of customization. Sticker Star and Color Splash are games that want you to play in a very specific way, and don't really give you a lot of opportunities to make choices or see much character progression. HP upgrades are predetermined, you can't really customize your deck of cards since they're expendable, and boss fights are paint-by-numbers, forcing you to use very specific thing cards in order to win the fight. You don't have to guess what item you need to beat the boss, so it's a bit better than Sticker Star, but still isn't very fun. You are stuck fighting the boss in one specific way. Classic Paper Mario let you customize your character by using the badge system, which in addition to giving you special moves and abilities, it allowed players to play however they saw fit. Want to go on a low HP or FP run? Just invest in upgrading your badge points. Want to be ridiculously overpowered or underpowered? Equip the proper badges and you can. Want to try a no jump or partners only run? With a couple of exceptions, that's totally possible. Classic Paper Mario gave the player many options in how they wanted to build their character. Color Splash and Sticker Star don't. Now we've made many direct comparisons to the first two Paper Mario games, but the truth is, Color Splash doesn't have to be like its predecessors. The series can and should change over time, but if you're going to change the system, you need to end up with something compelling and rewarding. There is a version of the card and paint system that would be an improvement. It's just not the version in Color Splash. The lack of any progression and frustrating inventory-based combat could be resolved by replacing it with some kind of deck building system, like in Kingdom Hearts Chain of Memories, Baten Kaitos, wait, Baten Kaitos, do you know which one it is? I have no idea. Great. Or the Mega Man Battle Network series. A card system with a sense of permanent progression makes card collecting worthwhile and fun. I've seen some people

## Evolving a Genre - From TF2 to Overwatch ~ Design Doc
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=liO9KKgi5IU

If you wanted to take your favorite game and make it better, where would you begin? Where would you look for inspiration? What steps could you take to improve something that's already fantastic? There's the perfect game to study if you wanted to answer these questions. Blizzard's Overwatch. Overwatch took an amazing class-based team shooter, Team Fortress 2, and through years of work and dozens of design decisions, it created a new state-of-the-art for the genre. Let's take a deep dive on Overwatch and see how it builds on the success of Team Fortress 2. In 2007, Valve released Team Fortress 2 as part of the Orange Box. The game was a fresher, more up-to-date take on class-based team shooters with a bold new art style. TF2's original art direction was that of a realistic military shooter, but Valve would eventually retool its look and replace it with the style as seen in the final game. As graphics improve over time, TF2's stylized look has kept itself from looking dated in the decades since, even without a major graphics update. Other games released around the same time as TF2 without that strong art direction haven't aged nearly as well. You don't exactly hear about how amazing Haze or Army of Two look now, do you? First, let's get the easier steps out of the way. Any game benefits from improving graphics, sound, and gameplay. So how did Overwatch improve on TF2 in these categories? Blizzard, like Valve, chose to give Overwatch a very strong art direction. Stylized, bright, and cartoonish. The art of Overwatch should stand out for years to come. Overwatch has a greater level of environmental detail in each map, which gives each location a more unique feel. For example, look at all of the objects to destroy and mess around with in the spawns of Hanamura or in Dorado. And then look at the simpler, more barebones spawn rooms of TF2. Overwatch also had more variety in its maps, whereas TF2 had maps mostly set in industrial desert environments. Which, while cohesive, it was a bit monotonous. Now what about characters? Both Overwatch's heroes and TF2's classes are packed with personality from their designs, taunt animations, voice lines, and even weapons. But Overwatch takes things a step further with highlight intros, and perhaps most impressively, the way every hero moves. This is most evident in everyone's walk cycle, as they are unique for each character. The way a character moves in the third person matches with their view in the first person. Even in the first person view, they communicate the identity of the player. Lucio feels like he's skating around, Bastion and D.Va feel heavy and robotic, Genji sounds light on his feet like a ninja, and Junkrat looks and sounds like he's limping. Most of the walk cycle differences in TF2 are just faster or slower. They're not very unique from each other and they don't really convey their personalities. Really, their weapons just sort of bob up and down and they don't really match with how they move in the third person. Moving on, Blizzard has also added a ton of graphical polish in other areas. Look at the HUD. A silky smooth ultimate ready animation, timers that blink when skills become available, flashy graphics for when the round ends. Overwatch also pays a lot of attention to detail in the typography and layout of its menus. So, instead of something big and dramatic, it's Overwatch's little improvements here and there that make it a higher quality graphical experience. What about improving on TF2's sound design? Instead of just adding more lines of dialogue or improving audio quality, Overwatch uses sound differently to improve upon the core gameplay. The gameplay in a class-based team shooter rewards teamwork. It's right there in the name. Overwatch is no different. The quickest way to lose a match is to charge in alone into the front lines. So, how do you encourage teamwork? In a game where the team with the best communication often wins, your team can do a lot better by just bumping up the amount of communication. What if the game automatically called out events? TF2 sometimes does that, as there are callouts for pushing the cart, when someone is on fire, if someone is capping a point, and other situations. Overwatch adds to this idea. Players will hear when teleporters exist, and they will also hear unique voice lines for when ultimate abilities are in use. Having automatic callouts lets you get more information out of teammates that can't or won't use a microphone. Character voices, footsteps, and other action sounds are also more dynamic in Overwatch. They change, not just by how far away you are from the source of the sound, but also how important the sounds are. For example, the ultimates of your enemies are significantly louder than those of your allies. All of this dynamic audio lets you concentrate on what the other team is doing, without as many distractions. What about gameplay? Class-based team shooters revolve around the game's characters, their movesets, and how they're balanced with each other. To improve a game like this, you might think you could just add more classes. And Overwatch does do this. There are over double the number of classes compared to TF2. But Overwatch mixes and matches classes and adds some new mechanics and new combinations of abilities to make the range of characters better. Overwatch's roster starts with many close parallels to many of TF2's classes. Mercy as the medic, Junkrat as the demoman, Torbjorn as an engineer. But then you add some twists to other TF2 classes. Pharah is a soldier with easier mobility, Bastion is a fragile heavy with a bit less mobility, Hanzo is a sniper with wallhacks, and after that, they create entirely new characters by mashing together specialized TF2 loadouts. Lucio and Pharah take the Pyro's pushback mechanics, Genji can use reflect mechanics like a Pyro and can double jump like a scout, Symmetra can shield players which is similar to how the medic can overheal, and she also gets the engineer's teleporter. Reinhardt's charge is similar to that of a demoman's charge, and a character like Zenyatta can damage at range, debuff, and heal all at once. Lastly, Blizzard adds in totally new mechanics to make even more characters. With area healing for Lucio, Soldier 76, and Ana, completely unique barriers for Zarya, D.Va, Winston, and Reinhardt, Winston gets a no-aim weapon, you can change your opponent's mobility with Mei's freeze gun and Lucio's speed boost. Even without coming up with all that many new mechanics, you can still get a lot of fresh-feeling character designs by mixing and matching like this. So far, we've talked about how Blizzard has improved on TF2's graphics, sound, and gameplay, but that's usually not enough to make a new game really stand out from its predecessors. There are plenty of new games out there that have taken beloved older games, improved on its graphics or improved on gameplay mechanics, and have still struggled to really catch on with players. To really stand apart from TF2, Overwatch came up with its own setting and its own themes. Instead of a 1950s Cold War setting, the backdrop is a near-future Earth set after a robotic uprising, where a supergroup of specialized fighters try to rebuild their reputations in order to save the Earth once again. That's simple enough to do, but in changing the setting, all of a sudden, some of the design decisions made in TF2 might not work in the context of Overwatch. Blizzard needed to identify and fix these problems to make Overwatch feel cohesive. To see how a difference in a game's setting can cause design changes, let's take a look at an example, character skins. TF2 has a strong red vs. blue theme that sticks to in its uniform design. Characters wearing uniforms make sense in TF2's lore, but Overwatch, on the other hand, treats its characters more like superheroes, and therefore doesn't have to use uniforms in its character design. Plus, if characters in Overwatch don't have to wear a uniform, then you can do more dramatic costume changes than you did in TF2. Dropping uniforms also presents a design challenge. If the characters in Overwatch don't have to look like their team members, and players on opposite teams can look like each other, then how do you know who to shoot? To solve this, Blizzard outlines all opponents in red, and makes it so that you are always fighting against the red team. A simple but effective solution. The designers of Overwatch broadened the range of character designs that would feel like they fit in the game, opened up an opportunity to customize and make money with cosmetic items, and changed how some of the core gameplay has to work. Three significant changes about character costumes, all caused by the change in setting. We've seen how Overwatch improves on what TF2 does already, and how Blizzard made their changes fit into the new context of Overwatch, but there has been eight years of new games and new ideas since the release of TF2. So let's take a look at some other popular games for more improvements. First of all, each character has their own abilities, cooldown timers, and ultimates, very similar to that of a MOBA. The character design in Overwatch is also very heavily inspired by many common tropes found in MOBAs. The best example of this would be Roadhog, who serves the role as the hook character, similar to that of Pudge in Dota 2, or Blitzcrank and Thresh in League of Legends. Instead of using TF2's static kill screen, Overwatch uses kill cams, similar to that of Call of Duty. There are also tons of games that have separated their serious and less serious player pools into different game modes, which helps everyone get

## Teaching Game Mechanics Well - Guidance VS. Hand Holding ~ Design Doc
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIs5189lmRA

Every designer eventually has to solve the same problem. How do you efficiently teach players how to play your game? Every designer solves this problem a little differently, but all solutions walk a fine line. On one side is under-explaining your game, where parts of the game's systems and mechanics are left as a mystery to the player. Although this can be used to great thematic effect like in the Dark Souls series, it's pretty unusual to see. Much more common is the other side of the line. The over-explanation. The hand-holding tutorial. The mechanical training wheels. The flashing neon solution. We've all had those moments in games like Pokemon or Zelda where we come across a section where we understand what to do and how to do it, but the game interrupts us to explain obvious things with long text boxes and choice-free tutorials. Becoming more of a wet blanket on the game's pacing rather than a helpful guide. A game that plays itself may as well be a movie, but a game that just immediately throws you into the deep end without easing you into it can be overwhelming or frustrating. Sometimes, without solid guidance, we become lost. But for the designers that can thread the needle, their works can become instant classics. Those fantastic pick-up-and-play experiences that are celebrated as some of the best that the industry has to offer. Games like Super Mario Bros., Mega Man, and Portal seamlessly teach their players while still challenging them. These games often teach players new mechanics not through text, but through what's called the isolation principle of game design. In practice, the isolation principle tends to follow three steps. Step 1. A gameplay mechanic is introduced in a safe, controlled environment. The player is usually not punished for any mistakes. Step 2. The mechanic is developed through more challenging examples with the safety floor removed. Step 3. The mechanic is combined with other established mechanics to create brand new challenges. The isolation principle is an efficient tool for quickly teaching new concepts in a more intuitive way and most importantly, it doesn't interrupt the game's flow. You don't need a game to constantly chime in to remind you how something works. Most Mario games use this constantly in their level design. Let's take a look at Super Mario 3D World, where we have a perfect example of the isolation principle in World 5-6, Cakewalk Flip. This stage uses all three steps of the isolation principle to introduce the player to platforms that flip as the player jumps. The level introduces this mechanic with a safety floor beneath it, so the player is able to approach this obstacle without too much pressure. After this introduction, the mechanic is developed with a couple more challenging examples with the safety floor removed. After passing these challenges, the stage mixes things up by throwing in another mechanic on top of the flipping panels, which in this case is an enemy that sends out shockwaves, challenging the player to think more carefully about the positioning and timing of their jumps. Going beyond Mario, Portal is another game that is so masterful at using the isolation principle that even though it's a game that is 90% tutorial, it never really feels like that because just like with Mario, it presents its lessons as mechanical challenges. The isolation principle unfortunately is not something you can just throw in without any thought. Some genres naturally make it harder to use effectively. Turn-based strategy games and RPGs usually have very complex and abstract mechanics, which makes it tougher to use. A game like Civilization, for example, might need to fall back on more basic teaching techniques, like text-heavy instructions to teach players how to play. It's tough to get statistical mechanics like happiness or science across to the player without just directly explaining it. You can also completely screw up using the isolation principle if you feed mechanics to the player too slowly and hold back the interesting parts for too long. Case in point, Final Fantasy XIII. Final Fantasy XIII is the poster child for too much hand-holding. It's infamous for its aggressively linear nature, to the point where some actually label it as Final Hallway XIII. Now, you'll often hear fans say that FFXIII gets good after about 20 hours. Why does it take 20? Why can't it be good in the first 5, or better yet, why isn't it good in the first hour? Very few games get away with taking that long to get going, and even other entries in the series don't have this problem. Even other very linear entries like Final Fantasy X. So what's so different about FFXIII? Here's another way to think about it. What is it that clicks after 20 hours? It turns out that that's about the point where the game finally lifts its restrictions on the player and lets them fully use the systems that it had been slowly teaching the player up until that point. So, in the first half of FFXIII, there are no towns to explore, NPCs to talk to, or minigames to play. Practically, all you can do is move forward from point A to point B. Now, that in itself is disappointing, but you can imagine that there could still be a good Final Fantasy game without as much exploration as you find in other games in the series. The game could have really focused on other aspects, like its combat system, but this too is bogged down by hand-holding. Combat in Final Fantasy XIII isn't like other Final Fantasy games where you select commands for individual party members. Instead, you only have full control over the party leader. Now, I say full control, but most of the time, you'll be using the auto-battle command, which picks commands for you. The auto-battle command does take away player agency, but the designers have tried to mix some back in through the paradigm system. As a new twist on the class job system of older Final Fantasy games, paradigms are the core of FFXIII's combat. Paradigms are sets of combat roles that your characters serve. There are six roles in total, and each character is naturally built to support three of them. In between battles, you can save up to six paradigms by mixing and matching these roles in any combination. During fights, you can then pick between your six paradigms in accordance to how the battle is going. For example, one paradigm could be a balanced party of a warrior, a mage, and a healer. Another could be more defensive with a tank, a healer, and a buffer. Or an all-out offensive paradigm could consist of one warrior and two mages. Micromanaging characters isn't the focus of FFXIII's combat. Rather, it's about the broader combat strategies through the paradigm system, which puts a ton of importance on who out of the main cast of six to bring to each fight and which roles they should have. Once you see that depth and complexity and start playing around with the system, Final Fantasy XIII's combat can be surprisingly fun and strategic, but the paradigm system only works when you're working with a full party of three. Early on in the game, the story forces you into parties of two, and later even when there is a party of three, it keeps you from swapping out members of the party, which really limits your options. And when is it that you regain full control over your party? About 20 hours in. No experimentation means no choice, and no choice means enemy hordes are BORING to fight. For 20 hours. That's insane. I wouldn't exactly call the combat simple to understand, so it does make sense that the first couple hours would restrain the player's agency, but the system isn't so crazy that it should take that long for the game to give you full control, which makes Final Fantasy XIII a tough game to stick with while its story gets up to speed. Restricting gameplay systems is just one form of hand-holding. Sometimes making a solution to a problem too obvious can be just as bad. This happens all the time, even to the best of games. So, let's take a look at how very obvious solutions can affect the Zelda series. Now, most 3D Zelda games are actually very good about teaching you concepts through gameplay, but they can also do this to a fault as they don't really challenge you to think outside the box. Most 3D Zelda games are infamous for the use the dungeon item to win problem. This is especially common with boss battles, particularly those in Twilight Princess and Wind Waker. Let's just say if boss battles are meant to be a game's big test, then too many Zelda bosses forget to hide the answer sheet. A boss with an obvious weak spot in itself isn't the problem. The bosses in the Dark Souls series are rarely about figuring out exactly how to hurt them and more about learning their patterns, properly timing your attacks and positioning yourself. The difference is in the player's execution. Most Zelda bosses are treated more like puzzles than actual battles. Attacks are easy to dodge and rarely do much damage. So it's less about execution and recognizing patterns and more about solving the puzzle of getting to the boss's weakness. The problem is that the solutions are more or less screaming at you the moment you see the boss. How many times is the weakness going to be a giant glowing eyeball? Or a giant glowing whatever this is? Having a consistent visual design is usually a good thing, but having an almost identical solution to the how do I kill this boss question can get dull. The first boss of the 3DS remake in Majora's Mask may be one of the worst examples of this. Adolwa... wait a minute, is that really how that's pronounced? Can we... can we just add a syllable in there? Make it a little smoother to say? Maybe unjumble it? No? Okay. The boss of the Woodfall Temple is in a room filled with these special flower launch pads, which the player can use with Deku Link to fly and drop bombs below. Now up to this point, the player has spent several hours using Link's Deku form, so the player is drawn towards these flowers. In the boss's introductory cutscene, we are shown

## Sonic & Gameplay Variety - How FOCUSED Gameplay Improves a Game ~ Design Doc
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qGM-dPerv1A

Video games can serve as an escape from the ordinary, the monotonous, the common everyday events that make life dull. New and different experiences let us escape, explore, and have fun. But while putting variety into your game is important, game designers need to be careful. Creating a range of experiences shouldn't turn the game as a whole into an underdeveloped, forgettable mess.
