There is a fine line between variety and aimlessness. Having each distinct experience reflect a cohesive whole is the goal. Do it right and you get WarioWare, Grand Theft Auto, or The Witcher 3. Do it wrong and you get Carnival Games for the Wii. But no series underscores just how tricky it is to add gameplay variety quite as much as Sonic the Hedgehog. For over two and a half decades, developer Sonic Team has tried over and over to add gameplay variety through different gameplay styles. With, well, mixed results. What is generally considered the core of a Sonic game? Going fast and momentum-based platforming. To let the player go fast, level designers need to make very large levels which are also challenging and interesting for the player to blaze their way through. For developers, this can be a design nightmare as it requires a huge amount of development resources for a relatively short amount of gameplay in a single stage. Because of how expensive it can be to make this kind of level, a full Sonic-focused game is by design pretty short. This is partly why many Sonic games feature multiple playable characters that go through the same or at least similar stages with different styles of gameplay as a means to lengthen the game and add variety. The earliest and perhaps smartest use of multiple characters in the Sonic series can be found in Sonic 3 and its companion game, Sonic & Knuckles. Sonic 3 & Knuckles presents the player with three different characters. Sonic, who provides the standard fast platforming that fans expect, Tails, who adds the ability to fly and swim to bypass some of the platforming challenges, and Knuckles, who trades some speed and jumping for the ability to glide and climb walls. What's great about the characters in Sonic 3 is that they let the player approach the same levels in new ways while still staying true to the core of a Sonic game. Tails and Knuckles don't play drastically different from Sonic, they work under the same general rules and have the same goals, the end of a stage. They just have a few advantages to provide for a slightly different experience, adding in replay value and variety while still keeping the speed and momentum that makes a Sonic game feel like a Sonic game. The Sonic Advanced and Sonic Rush series both use the same idea with different characters, and for the most part it works. While multiple characters were a solid way to bring variety and replayability for 2D Sonic games, how does this work in Sonic's jump to 3D? The original Sonic Adventure, released in 1999 for the Sega Dreamcast, featured six different playable characters, each with their own story and unique style of gameplay. These characters included Sonic, Tails, Knuckles, Amy, E-102 Gamma, and... Big the Cat. Sonic's gameplay consists of the fast platforming that players expect, Tails is similar, except that he has to race either Sonic or Eggman and retains his ability to fly, Knuckles changes the game up entirely with a treasure hunt for emerald shards in large open sandbox stages, Amy's story focuses on slower platforming while running from a giant robot, E-102 Gamma is based around shooting, and Big the Cat's gameplay is all about putting a fishhook through his best friend's face. As the years went on, the most divisive aspect of Sonic Adventure was these different characters and play styles. Developer Yuji Naka was wrestling with creating such huge worlds for Sonic. In a 1998 interview, he said, "...because Sonic's very fast, you have to create a huge-scale simulation. I put huge efforts into creating a big map. Of course I have to focus on the details of the 3D world, but I have to create a vast-scale map as well. This is the most difficult aspect of Sonic Adventure. If it were Mario or a slower character, I wouldn't have to create the huge world first for Sonic, but then thought, why not utilize these maps for other characters? Maybe I could add some variety to the game, not just running quickly through this huge world. That's one of the key concepts in the game." Now, using multiple characters in the same levels allows the developers to reuse art and design assets, which extends the game's length and adds in variety. But if it's not done carefully, it can dilute the focus of the core game. You can't expect the same level design to feel good for fast-paced platforming, extremely slow platforming, a treasure hunt, and a shooting gallery. Adding in a completely irrelevant fishing minigame with bootleg Totoro doesn't solve the problem. Forcing the player to slog through every one of these play styles to finish the game doesn't help either. This was a problem that Sonic 3 & Knuckles avoided because the characters were treated more like variations rather than completely different kinds of games. The stage design still felt intended for them. At times, the levels in Sonic Adventure can feel at odds with certain characters that the stages weren't originally intended for. Taking a level that works well for Sonic and forcing it to also accommodate for the shooting or treasure hunting stages can limit the design space for both gameplay styles. For example, the downtown section of Speed Highway is an area that feels designed for Knuckles, with a lot of verticality on top of having an open-world sandbox design, similar to that of Mario 64, with a ton of little nooks and crannies to explore while hunting for emerald pieces. Now Sonic goes through the exact same area at the end of his version of Speed Highway, but because of the verticality and open nature of the stage, it feels like a strange and abrupt place to end a level as Sonic, who's at his best when he's running through long stretches of terrain. The same problem applies to E-102 Gamma, where 80% of his stages are shared with Sonic. Because Gamma's moveset doesn't really work with the rollercoaster level design of Sonic, the developers gave him the smaller, flatter sections of those stages instead of building his own from scratch, which doesn't really work. Gamma's gameplay is based around shooting enemies to keep a timer from hitting zero, but the thing is, his stages are too small for this to even work. They're based around a timer, but really you don't need to shoot any enemies to make it in time, which makes his gameplay feel kinda pointless. Only Gamma's final stage takes any real advantage of his gameplay style, and it's the only one that wasn't originally built for Sonic. This issue was partially fixed in Sonic Adventure 2, where the six play styles are reduced to only three in the main game. Running, shooting, and treasure hunting. Stages are no longer shared between characters beyond some similar themes and art assets, so levels are designed with the respective play styles in mind. However, Sonic Adventure 2 still suffers from some serious pacing issues. Amongst other problems. Emerald Radar. Sega continued to experiment with the series by using other characters and play styles in Sonic Heroes, Sonic Unleashed, and the hilariously awful Sonic 06. All of which suffered similar problems. The additional characters and styles would become one of the focal points of criticism for Sonic from both fans and critics alike. So much so that the actual lack of them became a focal point for the marketing of Sonic 4. There was a general consensus that many people wanted more focus and polish put into Sonic's core gameplay, and aside from some of the handheld titles, it wouldn't be until 2010's Sonic Colors where Sega finally struck a balance between Sonic's high-speed gameplay, varied platforming, and exploration. Sonic Colors understands the core appeal of Sonic. It's not this. Or this. Or whatever the hell this is. Sonic Colors keeps itself focused on this. Taking what was learned from the daytime half of Sonic Unleashed, Sonic Colors is about racing your way through the stage as Sonic and only Sonic. The game seamlessly shifts perspectives between 2D and 3D, and every level keeps the player on their toes. By making them use Sonic's array of mobility-based moves with boosting, quick-stepping, drifting, homing attacking, and sliding. In addition to Sonic's large moveset, additional variety is created with the Wisps. Wisps are colorful creatures that serve as power-ups, granting Sonic special context-sensitive abilities that are built around the level design. There are a total of 8 Wisp powers, and they all share a common trait. Movement. White fills up the player's boost gauge, Cyan turns Sonic into a laser that bounces off of walls, Yellow lets him drill underground and underwater, Green allows him to fly and dash through trails of rings to gain speed, Pink grants the ability to scale walls, Orange launches him up to great heights, Purple turns Sonic into a monster that chomps its way through enemies and obstacles, and lastly, Blue lets him change special blue rings into platforms, and vice versa. Every Wisp power allows Sonic to move in ways that he simply couldn't before. They're rarely ever required to complete the game, and most importantly, they are easy to control and quick to use on the fly, with just a press of the button or a flick of the Wii Remote. These powers add in a slight Metroidvania style of exploration to the game, as they open the way to alternative routes and levels. For example, in the first stage, there are large sections of dirt designed for the Yellow Wisp, which is unavailable during the first playthrough. When the power is unlocked later on, the player can go back and explore these areas to see what they missed. These alternate routes often lead to one of the many hidden red rings, which unlocks bonus stages and eventually

## Directing Exploration - How Games Guide Players WITHOUT Tutorials ~ Design Doc
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rrL3iG_uacw

Atomic games are usually about going on some kind of journey, but how do we know where we're going? What do games do to point us in the right direction? Most games don't necessarily need to do a whole lot for players to have an idea of where to go, but the way to efficiently present this can depend on how linear or open a game is. The way most games are structured falls somewhere on a spectrum of two extremes, linear and open-ended. For the purposes of this video, we will be classifying games under three broad categories, linear, open-ended, and in between these two, semi-linear. On the linear extreme, we have games like Uncharted and Star Fox 64. These games are similar to theme park attractions, often taking players through elaborate corridors and set pieces. Traditional exploration is not really the focus of linear games. Instead, they're more about providing either a specific challenge to the player or unfolding a traditional narrative. On the open-ended extreme, we have games like Skyrim and Minecraft, which are usually large sandboxes where players are free to explore and engage with the world however they see fit with little limitation. For many of these games, exploration is the game. Now, between linear and open-ended games, we have what we'll call semi-linear games, which, as you might guess, are a mix of both worlds. The games that fall right in the middle under this category would include games like Dark Souls and Castlevania Symphony of the Night. Often the goals in these games are very straightforward, but there is an emphasis on exploration. The category a game may fall under can have a major influence on how it can efficiently direct its players. For the remainder of this video, we are going to take a brief analysis of three different games that each fit into these three categories. We will discuss how each visually directs the player on where to go within the first few seconds of gameplay. And interestingly enough, all three of these games can be found on the original Nintendo Entertainment System. These include Super Mario Bros., Metroid, and The Legend of Zelda. This holy trinity of Nintendo each fit within these categories and effectively convey their respective goals the moment that the player hits start. So, let's begin by taking a brief look at the original Super Mario Bros. One thing to keep in mind is that being a launch title for the original NES, Super Mario Bros. was designed as an introduction to video games for millions of people. And the way that it almost effortlessly teaches its players through level design alone reflects this fact. You don't need a manual to understand how to play Super Mario Bros., and the first screen shows us this. Notice where the player character is faced. On the left, facing right. The composition of this screen is saying one thing to the player. Go right. A thing that you'll be doing for 99% of this entire game. But what is really worth knowing is that once Mario moves towards the center of the screen, the camera begins to follow him, placing him at the center of the screen, which makes the purpose of the first screen more clear. This deceptively simple use of spacing at the start does wonders in literally directing a new player to move forward. Now with this knowledge, let's move on to our semi-linear game, 1986's Metroid. Now compared to Mario, how does Metroid start? It's a bit different, right? Unlike Mario, the player character, who is named Samus, is placed not on the left side of the screen, but at the center. Well, slightly off-center, but we'll come back to that later. Anyway, being at the center, the player is now presented with two paths, left or right. Let's pretend that Mario is the only other game we've played, so we stick to what we know and move to the right. Moving to the right, we encounter some enemies, make a few jumps, shoot through some doors, until we come across a space that is too small for us to pass through. We can no longer progress this way, so logically, we go back the way we came and take the path on the left, where we see a stairway and a space similar to the one that we saw earlier. Beyond the stairway, we find a small area with a flashing orb in the center. With no other options, the player naturally goes to collect the orb, which gives us a new ability to change into a ball form, which is our only way out of both here and the area that blocked us earlier. And already, Metroid has established the core of what the player does for a majority of the game, progress through the world in a somewhat linear fashion while exploring the available areas for hidden paths and new abilities to get even further in the world. All without the player ever needing to look at the manual or read a piece of dialogue. And going back to the first moments of the game, remember how Samus was placed off-center to the left? Well, that was a subtle way to nudge players into the direction of the power-up, which would save the player a few seconds if they chose to go that way. While there is a linear progression to Metroid, it's a game that you can only progress by exploring every nook and cranny for new abilities to reach new areas, and this first area is brilliantly designed to get that idea across to the player. Now for our final example, we'll be looking at one of the first major attempts at open-world game design, The Legend of Zelda. Similar to Metroid, we are placed at the center of the screen, but now we look at the game from a top-down perspective. We have also upgraded from two paths to a whopping four. Left, up, right, and a black square that represents a cave. Based on the contrast of the cave entrance, the player is more likely to go here first. Inside the cave, the player is given a wooden sword which allows them to fight off enemies that they will encounter on every other path. If the player goes off without grabbing the sword, they'll likely come back here at some point whether they died or they feel that they can't handle the enemies out there. Now once the player has their weapon, they're free to explore a pretty large portion of the world in the pursuit of secrets, dungeons, and treasure. Now while this is somewhat similar to how Metroid was structured, there is way more emphasis on both exploration and discovery. There isn't really a straightforward path, and the opening screen reflects this nature. So now that we've gone over these three structures, we now know that depending on how a game is structured, whether it's linear or open-ended, should be reflected upon how the game presents itself to the player. Many of the fundamentals that these examples displayed have continued and evolved, from Mario to Crash Bandicoot to Uncharted, from Metroid to Symphony of the Night to Dark Souls, from Zelda to Shadow of the Colossus to Skyrim, the influence of level design and the sense of direction is still there and continues to evolve and change. Now at some point in a future video, I would like to dive into the nitty-gritty of the other ways that games direct the player, but for now, think about this. Next time you're playing a game, think about how that game might be leading you on, particularly if that game is open-ended. You might be surprised by just how subtle or direct a game can be.

## Mechanics & Character Design - How Mario & Dark Souls Communicate Characters ~ Design Doc
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Vopm0YjjQcE

Characters are a very versatile way to give games both mechanical and narrative depth. When used right, they're a very powerful tool for teaching game mechanics to players in an intuitive way. Even something as basic as the way characters look and move can give us context for who they are and how they function in the game. As an example, we are going to look at three basic enemies from the original Super Mario Bros. Meet the Goomba, the cannon fodder of Mario enemies. What is it about the Goomba that tells us that it's a threat? Well, those cartoonish angry eyebrows aren't exactly friendly looking, and the fact that the Goomba is moving towards the player does suggest opposition. In the later games, they would further reinforce its hostility by adding fangs to the design, a pretty goofy but effective touch. The Goomba also serves a very important role in teaching the player how to jump. The player cannot pass the Goomba without jumping, ensuring that they have to use this key ability. Besides just getting past the Goomba, there is also the possibility of the player landing right on top of it. If the player does this, the Goomba is then killed, which establishes jumping as your primary method of attack throughout the game. One other note to make is that the placement of Goombas throughout 1-1 also shows how the Goomba reacts to other objects and enemies in the environment. Unless there is a wall or another enemy in the way, the Goomba marches forward, even if it means falling into a pit. Moving on, the next enemy that the player is introduced to is the Koopa. Immediately, what draws our attention here is its round green shell, suggesting that this enemy is more resilient than the fragile Goomba. And like the Goomba, the Koopa moves towards the player, which solidifies the player's understanding of hostility in the game. Even though the Koopa doesn't look as angry as the Goomba, it's still marching towards you, looking for a fight. The unique trait of the Koopa is how it also retreats into its shell upon being stomped on, unlike the Goomba who just disappears. If the player then jumps or runs into this shell, it is then launched, sliding across the ground, taking out enemies and bouncing off walls, suggesting potential new strategies for the player. Although this shell can be dangerous if it hits the player from the side. Anyway, the last enemy that we'll be looking at is another turtle-like enemy found later in the game called a Spiny. The Spiny has a shell very similar to that of the Koopa, but the design difference serves as a counter to what we've previously learned. This is an enemy that screams, don't touch me, with the attention-grabbing red and the obvious spikes. While one could argue that for the Goomba and the Koopa it wasn't abundantly clear that the player could simply jump on top of them, the Spiny makes it very clear that you can't take it out directly and that it should be avoided. The genius of Mario's enemy design is that every enemy communicates many of its characteristics through its appearance, without explaining through text. Because of how it simply communicates behavior, it can quickly introduce new gameplay elements on the fly, without stopping to explain exactly what each new character or item does. Despite the graphical limitations of the NES, the developers of Super Mario Bros. were able to create a rather large variety of enemy types that all do a solid job of communicating their behavior through their appearance. If they could do all this with such limited hardware, imagine what we can do now. The increased graphical fidelity of modern hardware opens us up to so many more possibilities in our character design. While the tools change as hardware evolves, the design principles of conveying mechanics through character designs remain relevant and useful throughout. Better hardware doesn't necessarily mean better design, but it does give us more possibilities. One series that follows these principles particularly well are the Souls games, namely Demon's Souls, Dark Souls, and Bloodborne. Going forward, we are going to take a broad look at the enemies from the first Dark Souls. The Souls franchise is infamous for its high difficulty, but it's a game that I consider tough, but fair. It's a game that rewards the player for paying close attention to their surroundings and having good reflexes. It's also a game with an incredible amount of depth within its combat. The combat of Dark Souls is largely based around keeping a close eye on your opponent, watching for their attacks, and acting accordingly, via dodging, parrying, or counterattacking. While more visually complex, the enemies of Dark Souls follow the same design principles as Mario, in that every enemy conveys itself through its appearance. For example, the equipment that the humanoid enemies carry tells us just enough about how they fight. Guys with spears tend to have long-range thrusting attacks, archers attack from a distance, heavily armored enemies tend to be slow and unflinching, with devastatingly powerful moves. This design trend is also applied with the more monstrous character designs. Attack dogs rush at you, gigantic armored boars have an unstoppable charge, dragons breathe down fire, plant monsters hide in plain sight requiring a keen eye for spotting them, and that's just a small sample of the enemies in this game. Beyond just the physical appearance of enemies, Dark Souls is able to go more in depth with its character design thanks to something the NES simply couldn't have taken advantage of at the time, which is full animation. As stated earlier, reading the attack animations of every enemy is a huge part of combat in Dark Souls. Every enemy has a telegraphed animation, so it's up to the player to learn and recognize each one and react accordingly. If the enemy is going to do a thrusting attack, the player can block it. If it's going to be a large overhead swing, they need to roll out of the way. The animation also matches with the appearance of each enemy. For example, lowly zombie-like foot soldiers flail their weapons around, while fully armored knights gracefully swing their blades, conveying a sense of discipline and proper training in their fighting style. In Dark Souls, there is so much more emphasis on how an enemy moves, rather than just how it looks. There is a similar emphasis on animation in other games such as the 2009 reboot of Punch-Out or the Monster Hunter series. But regardless, in the context of games, it's incredibly important that our character design evokes what those characters can do. A strong character design can make even the most complicated of mechanics seem more simple.

## How Games Convey Pain - Exploring Life Bars and Feedback ~ Design Doc
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0zs_2eEyKTc

It can't be overstated how important the sense of pain and irritation is to us. Pain is the body's natural way of saying, hey, we have a problem, do something about it. Pain can also help us learn from our mistakes. Through it, we become more aware of the dangers around us. It's literally a case of whatever doesn't kill you, makes you stronger. So in short, understanding pain can be instrumental to survival, and survival in itself is a large part of what makes a lot of games kind of fun. In a majority of the games that we play today, death is often a constant factor. Whether it's fighting off hordes of zombies, aliens, or sometimes just straight up Dracula, the characters that we play as are often in the face of constant danger and opposition in order to make our games more exciting and engaging. So naturally, we need to be able to sense when we are in peril. However, in games, we don't and probably shouldn't experience pain. So the question becomes, how do we convey pain without pain? The most common and straightforward solution to this problem came in the form of a simple infographic known as the life bar. Making its debut in Nintendo's 1983 arcade hit Punch-Out, the life bar has been a staple aspect of game design ever since. While the specifics may vary from game to game, the life bar generally serves as a simple and easy to read representation of the player character's health. As the player takes damage or makes mistakes, the bar will decrease a certain amount. If the bar is ever empty, it will usually trigger a death or a game over, a type of fail state that will send players back to an earlier point in the game to try again. The way the life bar is presented to the player can come in many different forms. These commonly included bars, dots or icons such as the Legend of Zelda's heart system, circular gauges, numbers and percentages, and any combination of these. Some games tried adding a bit of narrative to their health bars, such as old first-person shooters like Wolfenstein 3D and Doom, which added little character portraits in addition to a number percentage. Many modern first-person shooters don't use a quantifiable health system at all. Instead, these games use more of a vignetting effect, which increases in intensity as the player gets closer and closer to the breaking point. Although the problem with this kind of health system is that it leaves players rather unsure about how much punishment they can actually take. Aside from vignetting effects, some games use the character themselves to convey its status. Super Mario Bros. in particular does this. In this game, you start out as regular Mario, where you're vulnerable and any hit you take is an instant death. However, if you collect a Super Mushroom power-up, you become Super Mario, increasing your size and allowing you to take an extra hit. And in the newer games, any subsequent power-up you collect also allows you to take an extra hit, upon which it reverts you back to your previous form. Regardless of exactly how it's implemented, the general simplicity of the life bar and its variants makes it a solid tool for informing the player of their status while still allowing them to stay focused on the actual game. This information also adds an additional layer of strategy to the game, letting players make risky decisions based on their status. However, just having the life bar alone might not be enough. Additional feedback is also important. If the player is taking damage and they don't notice or understand why they're taking damage in the first place, then that can be extremely frustrating when they suddenly die without knowing what was even hitting them. The last thing a game designer wants is for their audience to feel like their failure was completely out of their control when it actually wasn't. Therefore, feedback in addition to the life bar is incredibly important. So what is this additional feedback? Well, when we sense pain, we naturally react to it. If something pokes us in the eye, we'll probably rub our eyes. If something kicks us in the shin, we'll probably grab our legs. So games need to do something of a similar nature. There needs to be some kind of tell to let players know that they've taken damage. Thankfully, games have tons of options for providing this kind of feedback, from animation to visuals to audio, even mechanics. Some of the more pronounced ways of letting players really know they've taken damage can be found in the form of stuff like controller vibrations, or perhaps having the player character either stunned or knocked back upon taking a huge hit. Some games depict their player characters as tired when they're low on health. Sometimes characters will be hunched over in their idle animations, or their voice clips will sound more exhausted as they move about. Now, there are tons of ways to approach this problem, but what's important is that it has to make an impact. The appropriate tools need to be there so the player is aware of what's going on in their immediate surroundings. If these tools are not there, then you run the risk of your players getting so frustrated that they give up on your game. And we don't want that.

## Top 5 Partners You Could Do Without in Games
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2DcKBstM0HA

Ah! Oh, still held! Still being held. That's a great job. You've applied the grit, we're all fine. That's tremendous. If there's anything I know, games love giving people companions. And sometimes that's great. That's fucking teamwork! Other times, not so much. While some partners can sometimes totally make the experience, there are some partners that just make you feel like you'd be better off alone. Which is why I bring you the Top 5 Partners You Can Do Without. Now let me clarify some things. Not everyone on this list is a terrible character. Only most of them. There are actually a couple characters that I really like, but for as much as I like them, these are characters that I feel are either annoying, unreliable, or unnecessary to the game. Now with that out of the way, what's going on everyone? I'm Warbot and let's get started. Ghost Trick is pretty freaking sweet. In this game, you play as Sissel, a ghost with amnesia and sweet-ass sunglasses. At the core of Ghost Trick is an adventure game based around the idea of possessing and manipulating objects to your will. Most of the time, you go back 4 minutes before someone's death in order to avert their fate. And that's where most of the story progresses. Coming from the same guys behind Ace Attorney, you're going to meet all kinds of eccentric characters. You'll meet characters like an extremely excited Pomeranian, a swanky detective who dances at every moment, a talking desk lamp who is a talking desk lamp, and a stern, no-nonsense chief of police, who I personally like to call Adolf McJaws. And of course you have your spunky female red-headed sidekick, Lynn. Now don't get me wrong, just because Lynn is on this list does not make her a terrible character. Lynn is perfectly likable and fun and is even helpful at times. But as a partner, she has one major issue. She kind of dies. A lot. Oh, and before you scream spoilers in the comments, this happens in the first 10 minutes of the game. Hell, this happens 3 times in the first 5th of the game. Lynn's got the survivability of someone driving a Ford Pinto. And the game knows this. For God's sake, this character's music theme is called Red-Headed Target. Sorry Lynn, but you're unreliable. As dumb and cheesy as it sounds, variety is the spice of life. We all know this. The Final Fantasy mages sure know what I'm talking about. You have all kinds of different mages. You have your black mage, white mage, red mage, green mage, beige mage, cage mage, and of course, blue mages. But to be honest, blue mages are not exactly my favorites. Unlike the other kinds of mages, blue mages learn and use abilities from monsters. Now that sounds pretty cool, and it is. But the downside with blue mages is that depending on the game you're playing, they can be kind of a nuisance to use. Enter Final Fantasy IX's Quina. Or is it Quina? As a blue mage, how does Quina learn her abilities? Is it by studying her opponent's every move and then duplicating their moves with extreme precision? No, she eats them. But let me tell you, she is a picky eater. Trying to learn new abilities by eating monsters is like trying to catch a rare Pokemon. You have to get their health just low enough. Fuck! And speaking of Pokemon, look at Quina's design. It's like the horrific love child of a legatongue and Chef Boyardee. As far as her personality goes, Quina has only two things to her. Thinking about food and speaking in broken English. It should come off as no surprise that Quina is a flat, annoying character. But I have a theory. One of the lesser aspects of Final Fantasy IX was that it made a few infamous nods to Star Wars Episode I. I'm talking specifically about the scene right before the Necron fight. The Yoda quote. This nod makes me wonder if there were any other inspirations taken from Star Wars. Hmm. Nope. Can't think of anything. Chrono Cross. This was one of my first Japanese RPGs that I ever played. While this game is nothing like its predecessor, it's still a great JRPG with a crazy storyline, a really unique battle system, and a simply outstanding soundtrack. And of course, who could forget your loyal party members? You know, guys like that guy. You know, he had magic and a staff. Oh, and that guy. He had the thing with the thing. And, um, who? Okay, scratch that. No one remembers these guys. Yeah, one of the more defining aspects of Chrono Cross, you have 45 different party members. That might sound kind of cool at first, but there are some issues with that. Issue number one. Your battle team only has room for three party members. And one of those party members has to be the main character. So essentially, you only have two slots and 44 characters to choose from. That's absurd. Issue number two. Most of these characters have no significance to the plot and have very little character development. In fact, most of the time, you just simply recruit party members by really just talking to them. In most JRPGs, it's supposed to feel exciting and fulfilling when you get a new party member. It's supposed to, like, have some significance in the plot. Like, when you get a new party member, you're supposed to be like, Yeah, I got a new party member! Awesome! But in Chrono Cross, it's more like, Oh, another guy. Guess I'll add it to the pile. Issue number three. Just on a base level, the designs of some of these characters are just bad and dumb. They're ba-dumb. I mean, what better people to help you save the world than a fisherman, the fisherman's mom, a scarecrow, a turnip, a rejected beanie baby, and Isla's mom as a child? Wha- Issue number four. The stats and abilities of about 80% of these characters are hot garbage. These party members are just the ultimate example of characters you don't need. Out of the 45 party members of Chrono Cross, you're really only gonna use about 8 or 9 at most. While none of these characters are really that bad on their own, there's just such a huge volume of them that I might as well just put them in one big entry. But if you really need one character, I guess the beanie baby? I mean, look at it. Why would you ever use that? Where's everyone going? Bingo? If you've been living in a cave for the last 10 years and have not played Resident Evil 4, A, go play it, and B, there are only three things you need to know about Ashley Graham. Number one, she is the poster child for annoying escort missions. During these missions, I can guarantee you she will die at least three or four times. And no, not by the actual enemies. She's gonna get shot by you. She is the prime example of an attention whore. And by attention, I mean gunfire. I could not tell you how many times I would have my shotgun aimed at an enemy's head and then have Ashley pop up right as I pulled the trigger. Number two, she is worthless as a character. Just in general. The game begins with her as a damsel in distress and the game ends with her as a damsel in distress. And finally, number three, her favorite word is Leon. Leon! Leon! Leon! Help me, Leon! Help me, Leon! Help me, Leon! Did you know that according to the extensive research of our most celebrated scientific minds and scholars, approximately 99.8% of all life on Earth absolutely despises the annoying anura known as Slippy Toad? However, for how much Slippy is hated by pretty much everyone, myself included, I would much rather have freaking Slippy by my side than bloody Prince Tricky from Star Fox Adventures. Let me ask you this, how the hell do you make having a pet Triceratops suck? Simple. You make them the dinosaur equivalent to Scrappy-Doo. First of all, Tricky will not shut up. My dad's a king earthwalker and he'll bash you up! If for some reason you think Navi is annoying, good lord, you're gonna hate Tricky. Throughout the whole game, Tricky is going to spout out about five or six random phrases for what seems like every minute. I'm hungry! Wait! Wait! Wait for me! Somebody stop this shark claw! Prepare to hear that for the next ten hours. I guess he's not the worst voice actor in the game, but then again you could be Gilbert Gottfried with laryngitis and still be a way better actor than, well... Okay, I'll say it, Tricky. But that still doesn't make up for the fact that Tricky will never shut up. At least Navi had something useful to say. Tricky is just talking for the sake of talking. And while we are still on the subject of being useful, he is almost never useful. But is Tricky more useless than Slippy? Let's compare the two. Slippy is the Star Fox team's only mechanic, he can give you data on the enemy's health bar, and he can also give you items once in a while. And if he's too annoying for you, you can shoot him down. Tricky, on the other hand, his two most useful abilities are being a paperweight and being a shovel. Sure, he could also breathe fire, but it sucks. And you can also play fetch, which is good for, well, nothing. And unlike Slippy, you can't shoot him down. So yeah, Tricky is somehow worse

## Top 5 Games of 2012
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pqAO6iUTLXw

2012 was a weird year for video games. It was a year full of controversy, disappointments, and delays. But, that's not to say this year was not awesome. The games this year were some of my favorites of the generation. There were tons of new IPs and new ideas, and for the most part, they were executed pretty well. Now, before I start, I just want to make it clear that there were some games that I didn't get around to in time, that a lot of people are going to be like, Hey, why didn't you play this game? Those games include XCOM and Far Cry 3. I want to play those games, I really do, but I just haven't had the time to do so. But anyway, let's get started. I'm Warbot, and this is my Top 5 Games of 2012. Going to a party, Corvo? Is that what you dreamed of, all those months in Coldridge Prison while waiting for the executioner? Now, I'll be honest. When I first heard about Dishonored, I was a bit skeptical. With all the media and hype behind this game, I couldn't help but feel like they were setting themselves up for disappointment. But, thankfully, I was wrong. Dishonored is a fantastic stealth game with plenty of choice. The greatest thing about this game is just the number of different options they give you. Now, sure, you could play it as a traditional action game and just go, Stab, stab, stab, stab, stab, stab, stab, stab, stab, stab. But stealth is the real way to go. Now, to make your way around the city streets, you are given plenty of awesome powers such as teleportation, possession, and rats. Lots and lots of rats. With these powers and some additional tools, you are given total freedom in how you want to sneak past guards, and also in how you want to take care of your targets in both lethal and non-lethal ways. For example, do I take option A, infiltrate a masquerade party and silence my target with my trusty sword? Or do I take option B, lure her away from the party, knock her out, and then give her to this guy so we can, what I assume is reenact the movie Misery? Or finally, do I choose option C, storm in with rats? More and more rats. Choices, choices. Fuck it, I'm going with option B. Let's reenact Misery. Bye, have a great night, you two. I don't think there's anything more fun than total freedom. Out of all the games this year, I don't think there has been one more magical or charming than Journey. This game may very well have one of the most gorgeous art styles that I have ever seen in a game. You could take any screenshot in Journey, and chances are, it would make for a fantastic desktop wallpaper. I mean, look at this. Are you seeing this? That sand looks like gold. Gold! I love gold! And the journey itself is so amazing. You really gotta commend it to the people at That Game Company. They have successfully told a really emotional storyline without using any dialogue whatsoever. Now, the reasons why the story succeeds is thanks to an ingenious use of online multiplayer. Using communicationless co-op, you end up feeling a real emotional bond to whoever it is you're playing with, even though you don't have any form of communication aside from chirping at each other. And the fact that they make this work is pretty crazy. And pretty awesome. Now look, if you haven't played Journey yet, I encourage you. Pick it up on PSN, turn off all your lights, turn off all distractions, and let yourself go in this wonderful masterpiece. The Walking Dead. Holy crap. While waiting for every episode to come out throughout the course of a half year, I think I might have gone through just about every human emotion. Now, most of the time, story-heavy games usually have their gameplay and story almost completely separate. But not with The Walking Dead. Here, the story and gameplay are one and the same. The heart and soul in this game comes in the choices, the writing, and the characters. Characters like Lee, Kenny, Lily, Ben,
Hey Ben.
Hey.
See ya.
Yeah.
And of course, Clementine. Take note people, this is how you portray a child character. Not this little crap.
Please dad, can I have one? I would really love to have one.
Jason! Jason! Jason! Jason! Jason! Jason!
Or this.
Dinner, dinner, dinner, dinner.
But this. Throughout the entire story, you'll meet new characters, say goodbye to old ones, and form bonds with them along the way. This is where choice really comes into play. Your choices will have significant impact on the fate of certain characters, the way characters perceive you, and the overall tone of the story, even if the events themselves don't change that much as opposed to someone else's game. And without spoiling anything, the choices in this game are beyond effed up. There is no good and evil choice. It is all shades of grey. It is brutal and amazing at the same time. The Walking Dead actually reminds me of Demon's Souls a little bit.
What?!
What I mean is, Demon's Souls is the gameplay as The Walking Dead is the story. Both of these games will crush your spirit, let you rebuild, and then crush it again, over and over. And by the end of it all, you feel complete and you feel satisfied with your experience. Good luck with Season 2, Telltale. You're gonna need it. Borderlands 2. Sure, you could call it Borderlands 1.5, but man, I had so much fun with this game, playing for dozens and dozens of fun hours in the fun storyline, having so much fun in the fun co-op with my fun friends, and having so much fun, fun, with such a fun game, and fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, fun, സ്ലാസ്സിസ്സ്ന്ന്ന്ന്ന്ന്ന്ന്ന്ന്ന്

## Top 10 Kart Racing Tracks
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RgfvnMZaBmQ

Alongside platformers and Japanese RPGs, kart racers are my favorite kinds of games. Whether it's the King of Racers Mario Kart or just one of its many knockoffs, I love these games. But what makes a truly great kart racer are the tracks, of course. Now, quick rules. The tracks in this list are included based on their creativity, their design, and their overall impact on me as a gamer. And also, I'm only going to allow up to three tracks per franchise. So anyway, what's going on everyone? I'm Warbot40 and this is my Top 10 Kart Racing Tracks. When it came to kart racers in the PlayStation N64 era, you pretty much had three big options. You had a choice of Mario Kart 64, Diddy Kong Racing, and Crash Team Racing. Now granted there were other kart racers, but for the most part those were the big three. And between those three, the one that stood out the most as far as gameplay goes has to be Diddy Kong Racing. Now why is that? Simple. Planes! Unfortunately though, what Diddy Kong Racing lacked was in its track design. There wasn't so much anything wrong with it, it's just thematically, it wasn't super memorable. That doesn't mean this game didn't have its fair share of standout courses. Such as my personal favorite, Hot Top Volcano. This was a course that was designed with planes in mind. Flying between stalagmites in an active volcano collecting powerups and going through shortcuts was just so awesome. But whose idea was it to go inside this active volcano? Was it you Taj? I think it was you Taj. Don't hello friend me. This track is awesome, but I think what makes it so memorable in the first place is that extremely weird theme music. I think the song is telling me to become a hula puma. What the fuck? Crash Team Racing If you didn't own an N64 back in the day, this right here was your Mario Kart. And you know what? It had no problems at all at filling that gap. Now I'm going to be honest here, there really isn't that much to say about this game. It's just a very competent kart racer with great track designs, powerups, and an interesting boost mechanic. One of the highlight tracks in this game has to be Sewer Speedway. And let me tell you, the name's accurate. This track is like something out of Sonic Unleashed. You can go through the entire track boosting, with frequent shortcuts, great places to drift, and you know what? All the mechanics come together perfectly in this track. The only thing I can really say about this place is that it's like there's an inherent rule that you always be boosting in this track. Like in the speedruns for this. Great, now I have to feel bad about myself. Now I'm no extreme sports fan, but if there is anything I love, it's a good snowboarding game. With two of my favorites being SSX, and Snowboard Kids. Yeah, Snowboard Kids. Anyone remember this little gem? As a kid, I adored this game, but I felt like no one ever really knew about it. I never heard anyone ever talk about it. And you know what? That's a shame, because this little gem rivals Mario Kart if you ask me. You just take a simple concept like Mario Kart, and apply it to snowboards. Bam! Award winning idea. You know, for a game called Snowboard Kids, you pretty much expect everything to be on snow, right? Well, you are wrong. One of the best tracks in the game is Grass Valley. No snow here. That don't make no sense! Nonsense aside, this track had countless variety. It starts you at the very top of a mountain, where you make your way down to the town below with multiple forts in the road, including a mine, a cliff, a forest, a meadow, and even a sunflower field. There is just so much variety in this track. And all while you are doing this, you are listening to one of the best tracks in the game. You would have to be heartless to not have a smile on your face now. This track is just pure bliss. But you know, looking at this, those kids do not care for proper physics. Or proper snowboarding gear for that matter. Is that girl wearing a bra? What do you get when you mix Mardi Gras, the Small World Ride, and all the drugs, and mix them together? You get Sunshine Tour. I'd be hard pressed to find any other courses that have a real party vibe to them. With this course's colorful backdrop and just vibrant atmosphere, it's a true party. And just like any other party, someone's eventually gonna spike the punch. Or in this case, open an interdimensional portal to God knows where. You know, the usual stuff. What? You guys are racing? Oh, that's cool bro. I'll just be over here tripping balls. Whoa. But seriously, I can't not put this on this list. I mean, come on, it has floating monkey heads. Why does it have floating monkey heads? I don't know. Video games? Okay, so like, some poser comes up to me with track suggestions for this list, and he's like, you know what's a pretty good track? Hot Air Skyway. And then I'm like, yeah, that was a pretty good track. That's all I got. Next. Despite all the different kinds of entertainment, we all still get bored once in a while. And when we get bored, we end up doing some of the dumbest shit. For example, I ended up watching Bait Car for three hours. Did I gain anything? No. Was it good? Hell no. I find the best solution for avoiding this dark, stupid path is to just go somewhere, like say a mall. Or you could be like Mario and hold a race at a mall. That's right, I'm talking about Mario Kart Wii's Coconut Mall. I don't know exactly what it is, but there's just something special about this place. The fun, outgoing atmosphere, the jumps, the multiple paths, even something about the three Miis at the end who must forever realign their parking job. This place is awesome, but come on, holding a race at a mall? That's just begging for a horrible accident to happen. What if some innocent bystander were to wander onto the track? Jason, no! No! No! No! No! Snowboard Kids 2 Aw hell yeah, it's BK2. Now this sequel just took what made the first one so great and just added more to it. More characters, more tracks, and less snow? Yeah, strangely enough, less than half of the tracks in this game are actually on snow. And let me tell you, these kids could care less about what they're racing on. Underwater? Do not give a fuck. In space? Do not give a fuck. In someone else's house at the size of ants? Do not give a fuck. But seriously though, Wendy's House. Out of all the entries on this list, this easily has the most nostalgic value for me. While the track itself is pretty simple, there is no denying its charm. With giant chocolate chip boulders, killer grandfather clocks, mouse holes, so much variety and creativity in this track, I love it! Makes me a happy Gilmore. Now you must be asking your computer screen, Warbot, what happened to the good old kids from down the block? Well they did make another Snowboard Kids on the DS, but we don't talk about that one. Lousy generic anime kids. Throughout the generations of mankind's existence, we have always found ourselves asking philosophical questions, some of which just do not have a true answer. What with those damn pinball tables that you cannot ever escape for the life of you. But in Sonic All-Stars Racing, this stage is king. Now just to be clear, I'm talking specifically about Roulette Road. Let's break this course down by doing the math. F-Zero plus Mario Kart divided by Sonic equals take all my money Sega. Whether it be on the original N64 version or on the remade Wii version, this castle still remains timeless and one of the finest examples of level design in gaming history. Now this stage had everything you wanted in a kart racing track. The visual style was memorable, it had perfect challenge to it like those swamps that would try to psych you out, it even had a rumor of that green thwomp at the entrance. ## Top Ten Worst Levels In Games
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZwGeYw6hslk

Regardless of what game you're playing, there's always that one level that makes you so excited just to be alive. It's like meeting an old friend who's got chocolate, puppies, and chocolate puppies. But with the yin comes the yang. Instead of that friend with the chocolate puppies, you have creepy Uncle Stanley with questionable stories. What's going on everyone, I'm WarBot40 and this is my top 10 worst levels. F-Zero GX is possibly my favorite entry in the franchise with the great rollercoaster speed, tracks, and music, but everyone knows this game is hard as balls. While the grand prix mode is a challenge to enjoy, the story mode enjoys stomping you with cleats. Now I am not kidding, after the second mission, the game becomes ruthless, the track designs become tricky and devious, enemy AI becomes super aggressive, and mission objectives are evil. They expect so much out of player ability that mission 6, it becomes the movie speed of all things. Apparently Captain Falcon's arch nemesis, not Batman, has dropped a bomb to our machine and now we have to make our way down the world's worst highway ever designed in the middle of rush hour. You let your speed down even once. I tried this over and over again, but with no success. Eventually I just gave up because the reward isn't really that great. Just a couple mediocre cutscenes. But you gotta give props to anyone who's actually finished this monster. Alright, so you're playing Mario Party with your friends, you're laughing, you're screaming, you're racing for those stars, you're having a great time. But unbeknownst to you, Mario's disembodied right hand has a heinous scheme. It wants the hands of others to suffer the same fate it has. And in order to do so, it lands on one of those minigames, you know the ones, Paddle Battle, Deep Sea Divers, Tug of War, Castaways. All of these minigames had a common control scheme. You had to rapidly rotate the control stick in order to be the winner. However, due to the design of the N64's control stick, a lot of players ended up getting a lot of blisters because the way it was shaped, there was a whole bunch of ridges that would cut into your hand. This got so bad that Nintendo actually had to give out gloves to anyone who ordered them at the time in order to avoid any possible lawsuits. That fact alone makes the control stick minigames more than worthy to be on this list. You win this round, Mario's dissevered hand. But I got my eyes on you. Aside from Half-Life, Halo probably has one of the best story campaigns in a FPS to date. The pacing, the weapons, they're all great. And of course, who doesn't love doing this? Hey, come back here, I just want to talk to ya! So I'll be satisfied. Of course, with every Halo entry, there comes the inevitable flood level. I'll be using Cortana as my example here, but there tends to be a general checklist that flood levels go through. Number one, lack of weapons and ammo. Number two, boring level design and aesthetic design. And number three, irritating enemies and those goddamn prego zombies. You know the ones I'm talking about, the ones that explode? Ugh, I hate those things. Damn pregos. You're probably wondering why I don't have the library from Combat Evolved on this. Well, simply, I didn't finish the story campaign in Combat Evolved. But I think we can all agree, the flood freaking suck! Yeah, that. Pikmin 2 has some truly amazing atmosphere. It truly evokes a sense of helplessness like you're just some tiny little bug in this large, mysterious, intimidating world. Even with a full platoon of Pikmin, you never feel fully prepared, as just one unexpected attack could cost you your entire army. In the perplexing pool, there is a dungeon in the middle of a southern lake known as the Submerged Castle. This area is only accessible to blue Pikmin along with some purple and whites waiting below, as well as some boltmen. Now, the actual level layout isn't anything special, but should you take too long on any floor, you get this. Say hello to the Water Wraith, an uncanny water frog that rides upon two stone columns that act as steamrollers. It is one of the few creatures that actively hunts you down. It is completely invincible and anything in its path is crushed and killed instantly, making this one of the deadliest creatures in the series next to the Smoky Prog. There is only one way to kill a Water Wraith. At the final floor, you have access to Purple Pikmin. You must throw the Purple Pikmin onto the Water Wraith, which apparently solidifies it. It doesn't make much sense. But even when you have it completely harmless, it's still creepy as hell. The Water Wraith truly evokes that aforementioned feeling of helplessness, and when it's all over and done with, you hope to never go back to its lair again. But, you know, I can't help but think the Water Wraith as what it would be like if Jaws could go on land. Hey guys, you ever thought about the greatest gameplay idea ever? How about making you stand still and jump for five minutes? And when we're feeling really creative, we make you run on this wheel for ten minutes. And make you enter a ten-digit long code. And then there's your level. Let me just say, we've done a good job here. Okay, I think we all know why this is here, right? But let's just ignore the obvious reasons why this is so flawed, and let's all just pretend that we are all aficionados of Disney music. I mean, you can understand why they went for a level like this in the Kingdom Hearts game. I mean, after all, Disney is the undisputed king of animated musicals. Now, The Little Mermaid had a lot of potential to be a great musical level. There are plenty of songs to choose from from that film. But out of the five songs used for Atlantica, only two of them were actually from the original film. Those being no-brainers like Under the Sea and Part of Your World. But the list is missing classics like Kiss the Girl or Poor Unfortunate Souls. Nope, no classic songs for us. Instead, we get original songs like Swim This Way. Swim this way, we'll dance and we'll play. Now it's very easy, come on in, just take a chance and shake a fin. Let the music move you. Oh god, my ears. They're gone. What if you took everything about the Water Temple and sprinkled on a little something
to make it just a little bit worse?
The result being the Water Temple Majora's Mask Cousin, the Great Bay Temple.
What the Great Bay Temple did that the Water Temple didn't?
Well, for starters, underwater controls.
Like, what you see?
Guess what?
It controls just as well as it looks.
Yep, no better way to go through a confusing dungeon than with even worse controls.
And also, instead of changing the water levels, you actually have to bring power to a whole
bunch of random gears.
And just when you thought this wasn't fun enough, wait until you hear about how you
actually have to get to this temple.
Nothing more than going on a painful scavenger hunt for Zora eggs, which you use to teach
you a song to open up the Great Bay Temple.
And after all that effort, you immediately go back in time to reset the three-day cycle,
undoing everything you've done to collect those eggs.
Sorry babies, you don't get to be born.
Now take everything I mentioned and compare it to the Water Temple.
Doesn't seem so bad now, right?
I mean, it still sucks, but relatively speaking.
